Point-and-Play: Instrument Timbre Cloning from Music Mixtures
Baotong Tian
Zhiyao Duan
Abstract
Neural instrument synthesizers can clone the timbre of a solo instrument, letting music producers make music with the sound they desire. However, an instrument of interest is often embedded in a fully produced, multi-instrument recording, beyond the reach of existing methods. Source separation before timbre cloning is an approach, but it may suffer from separation artifacts and is also likely a detour for the task. In this work, we propose Point-and-Play, a system that clones the timbre of a cued source directly from a polyphonic mixture and uses it to synthesize new pitches and velocities. To achieve this, we introduce a Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module that extracts the timbre code of the cued instrument from adapted CLAP embeddings of the music mixture. This extracted timbre code is then used to condition a separately trained note synthesizer together with pitch and velocity inputs. Experiments show that our proposed system outperforms separate-then-clone baselines in terms of timbre fidelity and synthesis quality, achieving comparable performance with that cloned from a clean solo instrument11

 Code and demo page are available at https://github.com/User-tian/Point-and-Play..
Index Terms: Timbre extraction, instrument synthesis, timbre cloning, audio representation learning, polyphonic music
††address: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, USA
1 Introduction
Neural instrument synthesis can render realistic notes from pitch and velocity controls, with instrument timbre specified by a text description or an isolated audio reference [22, 11, 37]. Instrument-specific systems have likewise improved the fidelity and expressive control of score- and MIDI-driven synthesis for piano [33, 27, 30], guitar [8, 16], and violin [10, 31]. A musician, however, may want to clone a particular instrument heard only within a polyphonic recording and use its timbre in music production. Existing approaches can isolate the desired stem through source separation [2, 19, 35], or replace the timbre of a source in a music mixture with a reference timbre [18], yet neither formulation addresses cloning the timbre of an instrument source from the mixture to synthesize new music content.
Figure 1: Overview of Point-and-Play. Given a polyphonic mixture and an audio or text cue, the system extracts the cued source’s timbre from the mixture and uses it to render new pitches and velocities.
Recovering a reusable timbre representation from such material is challenging because information about the target instrument is entangled with its pitch, recording conditions, and competing sources. A natural approach is to first separate the target source from the mixture and then apply a timbre cloning model designed for isolated references. However, many source separation systems are designed to recover a predefined set of stems [28, 2, 34], making them ill-suited to arbitrary instruments specified by a cue. Even when a suitable separator is available, separation artifacts can propagate to the downstream synthesizer and degrade timbre fidelity. Moreover, waveform reconstruction is an unnecessary intermediate objective for this use case, since the separated stem itself is not the desired output.
We therefore pursue direct mixture encoding, in which the target timbre is inferred directly from the mixture without the intermediate target reconstruction. The main challenge is to make this representation selective to the cued source while discarding both competing sources and source-specific musical content such as pitch, so that the resulting timbre can be reused to synthesize new notes.
We formalize this missing task as instrument cloning from music mixtures. Given a multi-instrument polyphonic mixture, the task is to clone the timbre of an instrument source cued by an audio example of the target instrument class or a text prompt containing its instrument name, and use it to synthesize music content that does not appear in the mixture. This distinguishes the task from timbre cloning from an isolated instrument recording, where the target timbre is directly observed without interference from other sources, and from text-to-instrument generation, where text specifies the desired instrument rather than identifying a source whose timbre must be recovered from a mixture.
To address this task, we introduce Point-and-Play, which extracts a cued instrument’s timbre directly from a mixture. Specifically, we propose Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP), which uses the cue to aggregate adapted CLAP [36] audio representations of the mixture into a timbre code. We train the extracted code to align with the CLAP embedding of the corresponding instrument in isolation, while encouraging invariance to musical content and selectivity to the cue. Our contributions are threefold:
1. 
We formulate a new task, instrument cloning from music mixtures, where a cued instrument is cloned from a mixture, and establish an evaluation protocol for this task.
2. 
We introduce Point-and-Play, the first system, to our knowledge, to clone a cued source from a polyphonic mixture toward synthesizing new pitches and velocities.
3. 
Experiments show that Point-and-Play achieves timbre fidelity comparable to instrument cloning from a clean audio reference while outperforming a separate-then-clone baseline.
2 Related Work
Text-to-instrument generation and instrument cloning aim to create reusable timbres that can be rendered at new pitches and velocities. Earlier systems derive instrument timbres from isolated examples [21, 7], while recent work has broadened timbre conditioning and improved the generative models. InstrumentGen generates sample-based instruments from text by combining a joint text–audio embedding with pitch and velocity controls [23, 22]. TokenSynth achieves this task by generating neural audio tokens from MIDI and CLAP-based timbre embeddings [11]. More recently, FlowSynth improves single-note quality and cross-pitch timbre consistency through distributional flow matching and test-time search [37]. Our system shares the goal of producing a reusable, playable timbre, but extracts it from a cued source embedded in a polyphonic mixture.
Music source separation instead reconstructs sources present in a mixture. Conventional systems target a fixed vocabulary, typically vocals, drums, bass, and “other” [28, 29, 2], a setup largely retained by newer architectures [1, 17, 34]. Target sound extraction enables user-selected sources via class labels or enrollment audio [3], language [15, 4, 14], and multimodal queries [19]. Recently, PromptSep supports open-vocabulary extraction and removal via language or vocal imitation [35]. For our task, one could first separate the target instrument and then clone its timbre, but source separation methods face a tradeoff between separation quality and source diversity.
3 Method
3.1 Cue-Conditioned Timbre Extraction
Given a polyphonic music mixture xmixx_{\mathrm{mix}} and a source cue, Point-and-Play extracts a timbre code zz for the cued instrument directly from the mixture. The cue can be an audio reference or a text cue, and the resulting timbre code is later used together with the requested pitch and velocity to condition the note synthesizer.
Figure 2: Point-and-Play architecture. A CLAP encoder fine-tuned with LoRA encodes the mixture, while a frozen CLAP encoder encodes the source cue. Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling combines both representations into a timbre code of the cued source in the mixture and uses it to condition the note synthesizer. During training, the isolated source of the mixture provides supervision; it is not required at inference time.
As shown in Fig. 2, the timbre extraction module consists of two encoding branches followed by a Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module. The trainable mixture branch uses a CLAP audio encoder fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [36, 6], which represents the mixture by a global code gg and token sequence H=[h1,…,hT]H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{T}]. In parallel, the frozen cue branch uses a CLAP audio/text encoder to map the audio or text cue into the shared audio–text embedding space, producing a cue embedding qq. CGSP then uses qq to selectively aggregate the mixture tokens HH to produce the final timbre code zz.

4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Data. The extractor is trained on polyphonic mixtures drawn from four corpora, namely NSynth [5], NLakh [12], Slakh [20], and MoisesDB [26], sampled with weights 0.30/0.30/0.10/0.300.30/0.30/0.10/0.30. For NSynth and NLakh, we randomly select four of 953 instruments and independently draw two sets of 4-second excerpts to form paired mixtures that share instrument identities but differ in musical content.
For Slakh and MoisesDB, the paired mixtures xmixAx_{\rm mix}^{A} and xmixBx_{\rm mix}^{B} comprise two independently sampled 4-second windows from the same song, retaining all available stems. Thus, all mixtures used for extractor training are 4 seconds long. All evaluations in Table 1, Figure 3, and Table 2 use 27 NSynth instruments held out from training. Figure 3 additionally uses an evaluation subset of MoisesDB excluded from extractor training.

Implementation. The mixture encoder is initialized from the HTSAT-base audio tower of a music-domain LAION-CLAP checkpoint [36, 13] and fine-tuned with rank-8 LoRA [6] (α=16\alpha{=}16) in every qkv, fc1, and fc2 projection; only the LoRA parameters and CGSP head are trained. The frozen cue and teacher encoders, as well as the candidate-selection embeddings, use the same music-specific checkpoint. For text-cued training and evaluation, each text cue is a coarse instrument-category name, such as “guitar”. All mixture views are cropped to four seconds during extractor training. We train the extractor for 18k steps with AdamW, a batch size of 16, and an InfoNCE temperature of 0.10.1. The learning rate is warmed up for 500 steps to 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4} and cosine-decayed to 3×10−53{\times}10^{-5}. Training takes approximately three hours on a single A100 GPU. The loss weights are λinv=λa=λt=1\lambda_{\rm inv}{=}\lambda_{a}{=}\lambda_{t}{=}1 and λs=0.25\lambda_{s}{=}0.25. The note synthesizer follows the FlowSynth latent flow-matching decoder [37], using a 24-layer DiT with a hidden width of 1,024, 16 attention heads, and AdaLN conditioning. The 512-dimensional timbre code is linearly projected to the 1,024-dimensional DiT width and summed with pitch and velocity embeddings to form the conditioning vector. The model predicts continuous latents in the DiffRhythm VAE space [24], which are converted to waveforms by the frozen VAE decoder. It is trained with the flow-matching objective in Eq. (4) for 150k steps using AdamW, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, batch size 48, and condition dropout of 0.10.1 for classifier-free guidance. Conditioning codes are extracted by the final encoder and sampled equally from NSynth note mixtures and NLakh phrases. At inference, we integrate 50 Euler steps from Gaussian noise and, for each conditioning code zz, generate N=8N{=}8 samples and retain the one whose frozen music-CLAP embedding has the highest cosine similarity to zz.
Comparisons. Table 1 compares four groups of settings or system configurations.
Oracle timbre. These settings condition the synthesizer with a Music-CLAP embedding extracted from clean recordings of the target instrument, setting oracle upper bounds. Specifically, target note uses the exact synthesis target note to compute the embedding, while target-instrument other note uses a different note from the target instrument. Cue timbre. These settings omit the mixture and simply use cue embeddings to condition the synthesizer. Specifically, text cue uses the name of the target instrument category,
target-category audio cue uses a recording of a different instrument from the target instrument category, and target-category centroid uses the average embedding of all training recordings in the target instrument category. These settings serve as baselines to test whether the cue (or average of cues) alone is sufficient to infer the target instrument timbre.
Separate-then-clone. These systems first separate the target source from the mixture and then condition the synthesizer using the Music-CLAP embedding of the separated source. These systems differ by their separation methods. Oracle ratio mask uses a mask computed from the ground-truth stem to separate the source. Demucs-closest separates the mixture into four stems using a pre-trained Demucs model [2] and uses the one whose CLAP embedding is the closest to the target instrument as the separation result. CLAPSep [19] embeds a text or audio cue in CLAP’s shared embedding space and uses it to condition a separation network that estimates a mask for extracting the queried source.
Point-and-Play. We evaluate three cue types for extracting a timbre code directly from the mixture: a text cue specifying the target instrument category name, a same-category audio cue from a different instrument in the same category, and a target-instrument audio cue from the exact target instrument.
In particular, the first two cues are most practical. For all systems, the synthesizer is trained to match the timbre space that the systems use.
Because the conditioning spaces differ, the oracle timbre, cue timbre, and separate-then-clone comparisons use a decoder trained on Music-CLAP embeddings of isolated sources, whereas Point-and-Play uses the same decoder architecture trained on timbre codes extracted from mixtures by CGSP.
Metrics. The primary metric is CLAP score, computed as the cosine similarity between each synthesized note and its synthesis target using a separate HTSAT-tiny audio tower of a general-audio LAION-CLAP checkpoint [36, 13].
FAD [9] measures distribution-level realism from VGGish embeddings at 16 kHz, and MSS is a multi-resolution spectral distance, with lower values preferred for both.

4.2 Evaluation Results
Playable-instrument generation from mixtures.
Table 1 reports the main generation results. Point-and-Play achieves a CLAP score of 0.7060.706 with text cue, 0.6780.678 with a same-category audio cue, and 0.6960.696 with target-instrument audio cue. These values are not far from the “target instrument other note” oracle of 0.7620.762, which shows that directly extracting timbre from the mixture with our proposed method can approach the performance of conditioning on a clean recording of the target instrument. Moreover, the two audio-cued configurations achieve an FAD of 1.921.92, close to the clean-reference oracle of 1.851.85, indicating strong distribution-level generation quality. Point-and-Play also outperforms all “cue timbre” methods in terms of CLAP score and MSS, showing the benefits of extracting the target-instrument-specific timbre from the mixture over using the timbre of a different instrument or the average timbre of the same category. Compared with separate-then-clone methods, all configurations of Point-and-Play outperform Demucs and CLAPSep across all metrics, suggesting that direct encoding preserves target timbre more effectively than the tested two-stage pipelines.
Pitch leakage investigation.
To assess whether the extracted representation retains the pitch observed in the mixture, we fit a five-fold cross-validated ridge regressor on held-out NSynth instruments to predict the MIDI pitch of the cued target note from the extracted timbre code, and report R2R^{2} (higher indicates more linearly decodable pitch information). The same probe achieves R2=0.783R^{2}=0.783 on raw music-CLAP embeddings of the corresponding isolated target notes, compared with R2=0.263R^{2}=0.263 on the extracted codes, indicating that the extractor suppresses, but does not eliminate, pitch information.
Mixture-duration study.
We evaluate mixture-duration sensitivity using decoder-free Recall@1, which measures whether the extracted code retrieves the correct clean target from a fixed pool of instruments. Figure 3 shows that two seconds is insufficient on both datasets, while four seconds captures most of the retrieval gain, and performance remains stable with longer context. For NSynth, each sample is a single four-second note, the result therefore indicates that one note is sufficient for retrieval. We therefore use four-second crops by default, consistent with the training window.
Loss ablation. Table 2 reports leave-one-out ablations of the full objective (Eq. (3)). All variants are evaluated using a single fixed decoder, trained exclusively on audio-CLAP embeddings of clean instrument recordings, ensuring that performance differences primarily reflect the encoder. We can see that the audio selectivity loss ℒsela\mathcal{L}_{\rm sel}^{a} improves the matched-cue CLAP score for both cue modalities while reducing the wrong-audio-cue score Wa from 0.4690.469 to 0.4300.430. It therefore enhances both target fidelity and selectivity to the audio cue. The instance-level losses are essential for preserving identity under their respective cue modalities. Specifically, removing ℒalgna\mathcal{L}_{\rm algn}^{a} reduces audio-cued CLAP score to 0.4170.417, close to the wrong-cue score, whereas removing ℒalgnt\mathcal{L}_{\rm algn}^{t} reduces text-cued CLAP score to 0.5780.578. In both cases, performance under the other cue remains largely unaffected, indicating that each loss provides modality-specific supervision. Finally, removing ℒinv\mathcal{L}_{\rm inv} degrades performance under both cues. This result suggests that encouraging timbre representation invariance to pitch variation improves timbre capture from polyphonic mixtures across cue modalities.
5 Conclusion
In this paper, we introduced a new task of instrument cloning from music mixtures and presented Point-and-Play, a system that turns a selected source within a polyphonic mixture into a playable instrument at new pitches and velocities. By extracting a timbre representation directly from the mixture, Point-and-Play approaches the performance of clean-reference conditioning and outperforms separate-then-clone pipelines. Future work will improve real-world generalization by scaling training to more diverse instruments and recordings and further assess perceptual quality through listening studies. Another important direction is to enable finer-grained source selection, particularly when multiple simultaneous instruments belong to the same category.

sections.body: 如果要复现，第一步不是直接训练合成器，而是先把数据与编码器管线跑通。按原文准备 NSynth、NLakh、Slakh 与 MoisesDB 的四秒混音与成对视图，NSynth 类用 953 件乐器中随机四件做混合并保留 27 件未见身份做评测，Slakh 与 MoisesDB 用同曲不同窗口做内容不同的配对。编码器从音乐域 LAION-CLAP 的 HTSAT-base 音频塔初始化，只训练 rank 为 8 的低秩适配与门控池化头，提示与教师编码器冻结，文本用粗类名，音频提示用同类不同乐器，错配负例用不同类音频。损失权重按不变性、音频对齐、文本对齐各 1、音频选择 0.25，总步数 18k，批量 16，温度 0.1，单卡约三小时。编码器收敛后再冻结它训练合成器，合成器是 24 层扩散变换器，音色码 512 维投影后与音高力度相加，训练 150k 步，批量 48，条件丢弃 0.1，推理 50 步欧拉积分加 8 选 1。评测时 CLAP 分数要用另一个通用音频检查点的 HTSAT-tiny 计算，不能用训练时的音乐检查点代替，否则相似度会被高估。关于资源可用性，没有确认作者资源当前可用，原文脚注给出代码与演示页链接指向第三方镜像，本次只验证到第三方链接可达，不能把它写成作者已开源或权重可下载，运行前需要自行确认仓库内容、权重与演示是否齐全。

styleSections.body:
主结果回答的是直接从混音提取是否值得做。论文报告在 27 个未见身份上，文本提示的 CLAP 为 0.706，同类音频提示为 0.678，目标乐器音频提示为 0.696，而用目标乐器另一音符做干净参考的上限为 0.762。数值差距不大，支持了从混音直接提取可以接近干净录音条件的判断。分布质量上，两个音频提示配置的 FAD 都是 1.92，接近干净参考的 1.85，说明生成质量在分布层面没有明显塌缩。与只用提示不看混音相比，所有直接提取配置在 CLAP 与 MSS 上都更好，说明混音提供了类平均或单个示例之外的具体证据。与已测的先分离再复刻相比，直接提取在各项上都优于 Demucs 与 CLAPSep，支持了跳过波形重建能更好地保留目标音色的解释。但理想比值掩码按真值分离仍有 0.726 的 CLAP，说明在分离近乎理想时两阶段也能很好，这也划定了直接编码优势的适用条件，即在实际分离器有伪影或词表受限时优势更明显。

下表把正文连续句子中有逐字证据的关键数字整理为五列，比较问题是直接提取与干净参考在目标相似度和分布质量上差多少，阅读时注意 CLAP 越高越好而 FAD 越低越好。

| 分组 | 具体条件 | CLAP分数 | FAD | 备注 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 直接提取 | 文本提示 | 0.706 | — | 来自混音的音色码 |
| 直接提取 | 同类音频提示 | 0.678 | 1.92 | 提示与目标不同乐器 |
| 直接提取 | 目标乐器音频提示 | 0.696 | 1.92 | 提示与目标同一乐器 |
| 干净参考上限 | 目标乐器另一音符 | 0.762 | 1.85 | 孤立录音条件 |

上表显示文本提示的 0.706 与上限 0.762 差距有限，而音频提示在 FAD 上与上限持平，代价是需要四秒混音证据与多候选挑选的推理开销。没有胜出的项也要看到，只用提示的基线与实际分离器基线都低于直接提取，但理想掩码仍高于直接提取，说明直接编码不是在所有条件下都最优。未评测的范围包括混音中目标极弱、严重掩蔽或多把同类乐器同时出现时的表现，正文结论不应推广到这些情形。

时长敏感性用无解码器的配对检索召回率来刻画，只改变中心裁剪时长。读图时先看横轴时长与纵轴召回率，再比较合成与真实数据的高度，最后看文本与音频提示的相对位置，重点确认四秒是否已拿到大部分增益。

[[FIGURE_3]]

图中横轴是混合时长从 2 秒到 8 秒，纵轴是检索召回率，橙色三角代表真实录音数据，蓝色圆点代表合成数据，实线是文本提示，虚线是音频提示。可见 2 秒在两个数据集上都明显不足，4 秒已经拿到大部分增益，更长上下文基本平稳。对 NSynth 而言每个样本是单个四秒音符，因此结论可读作一个音符的证据已足以支持检索。默认用四秒裁剪与训练窗口一致，复现时不应随意缩短输入，否则会落入 2 秒不足的区间。

What Does LALM Post-training Learn? 
Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
Hua-Hsuan Chen
Xuanjun Chen
Wei-Chung Lu
Chih-Kai Yang
Yu-Xiang Lin
Sung-Feng Huang
Haibin Wu
Hung-yi Lee
National Taiwan University
NVIDIA
Independent Researcher
NTU AI-Core
Abstract
Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks.
However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats.
Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes.
These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
1 Introduction
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rejection fine-tuning (RFT) Yuan et al. (2023), and reinforcement learning methods including GRPO Shao et al. (2024); DeepSeek-AI (2025) and VCRL Jiang et al. (2025) have become standard post-training recipes and have proven effective for LLMs. Recent work has also applied these methods to large audio-language models (LALMs), yielding substantial gains on benchmarks built for audio understanding and reasoning, such as MMAU Sakshi et al. (2025) and MMAR Ma et al. (2025b).
While post-training successfully improves overall performance, recent studies have made a surprising observation: certain gains can be achieved even without audio inputs Rouditchenko et al. (2025).
Therefore, it raises a fundamental question: does post-training actually improve audio understanding and reasoning, or does it merely rely on improved text-only capabilities to answer without listening?
Figure 1: Schematic overview of LALM post-training. The illustration demonstrates that models achieve comparable performance gains (e.g., ∼\sim+40) whether post-trained with informative audio (a) or silence (b). 
To investigate this, we must determine whether models genuinely utilize audio during inference, because a correct answer with audio present is inconclusive due to potential text-only shortcuts. To isolate the true contribution of audio understanding and reasoning, we evaluate both base and post-trained LALM models under different input conditions. As illustrated in Figure 1, our framework compares post-training performance when models are provided with informative audio (a) versus silence input (b). Building upon this controlled evaluation protocol, our study is structured around two core dimensions to thoroughly uncover what models learn. First, we examine the necessity of audio during both evaluation and training by introducing silence controls. Second, since post-training gains may stem from exploiting textual cues rather than acquiring genuine auditory capabilities, we further investigate whether these improvements depend on the multiple-choice format by removing answer options. To answer the overarching question of what LALMs actually learn during post-training, our analysis reveals three main findings:
• 
LALM post-training yields comparable performance gains regardless of audio and silence input. 
Our largest performance gains on MMAU and MMAR (+14.8+14.8 and +7.2+7.2 points, respectively) retain +11.2+11.2 and +4.9+4.9 points under silence, and models post-trained entirely on silence still improve on real audio.
• 
Most LALM performance gains are relied on the text question format.
When evaluated in an open-ended setting, models suffer severe performance degradation, maintaining negligible reported gains despite post-training.
• 
The audio-grounding performance gains of LALM are marginal.
Across different evaluation settings, improvements depending on audio input account for a negligible fraction, calling into question the model’s actual audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.
2 Related Work
Post-training for audio reasoning.
The post-training recipes now used on audio were developed on text, where their reported benefits were
established on mathematics and code, and they have been carried over largely unchanged.
Chain-of-thought prompting was examined first Ma et al. (2025a), then reasoning
traces trained at scale Zhifei et al. (2025), and reinforcement learning with
verifiable rewards now dominates: answer-level group-relative
optimisation Li et al. (2025); Rouditchenko et al. (2025); Zhao et al. (2025) and variants that
change the curriculum, the reward granularity or the training
data Wen et al. (2025); Diao et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2026); He et al. (2026).
In all these approaches, the reward function verifies only the final answer, providing no signal on how that answer was derived. Consequently, these studies primarily report overall accuracy, as it is the sole metric optimized during training. In this work, we hold the training setting fixed and investigate whether this accuracy stems from true audio reasoning or mere text shortcuts.
Whether LALMs listen.
Unlike text LLMs, LALMs must extract reasoning evidence from an audio waveform rather than text tokens. Since a correct answer can also be derived from the language model’s internal knowledge, higher audio-QA accuracy does not guarantee actual audio comprehension. Previous work has found that many benchmark items can be answered with no audio or silent audio Foo et al. (2026); He et al. (2026), revealed that models follow the text over the acoustic signal when the two disagree Wang et al. (2025), and shown that strong reasoning scores coexist with weak acoustic perception Zhang et al. (2026), which decays further as reasoning lengthens Mao et al. (2026). Post-training gains have likewise been traced to text-based reasoning Rouditchenko et al. (2025).
However, whether post-trained LALM models rely on the audio or text capabilities to answer remains unclear.
Standard evaluations based on absolute accuracy fail to capture this.
To address this gap, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol to isolate the true audio contribution from absolute accuracy.
By doing so, we shed light on what post-training actually learns, offering a principled way to rethink and evaluate audio understanding and reasoning capabilities in LALMs.

3 Controlled Evaluation Protocol
Audio and silence evaluation.
To isolate the audio-specific improvements of post-training, we evaluate each post-trained model under real audio and same-length silence input conditions, keeping text inputs constant and measuring performance relative to the base model.
Letting Acca\mathrm{Acc}^{a} and Accs\mathrm{Acc}^{s} denote the accuracies under real audio and silence, we define the performance gains as:
Δ​Acca\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{a}
=Accposta−Accbasea,\displaystyle=\mathrm{Acc}^{a}_{\mathrm{post}}-\mathrm{Acc}^{a}_{\mathrm{base}},
a:audio\displaystyle a:\ \text{audio}
(1)
Δ​Accs\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s}
=Accposts−Accbases,\displaystyle=\mathrm{Acc}^{s}_{\mathrm{post}}-\mathrm{Acc}^{s}_{\mathrm{base}},
s:silence\displaystyle s:\ \text{silence}
We refer to Δ​Acca\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{a} as Audio Gain, which reflects the overall performance improvement under standard evaluation, and Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s} as Silence Gain, which reveals how much of that improvement persists even in the absence of any audio input.
Multiple-choice and open-ended evaluation.
We evaluate performance on each benchmark under two answer formats: the original multiple-choice setting, where the model’s response is checked against provided options, and an open-ended evaluation, which removes these options and presents the question independently.
The model generates a free-form response, which is evaluated by an LLM judge for semantic equivalence to the reference. Since omitting options makes some questions unanswerable, the necessary rewriting rules and judge prompts are provided in Appendix C, with all other evaluation settings remaining unchanged.
4 Experimental Setting
Training data. 
The training data pool contains 12,267 multiple-choice audio QA items derived from Audio-Cogito Li et al. (2026) (using only the question and gold option).
These items cover 7,129 clips (17.4 hours) across three public corpora, representing distinct domains:
AudioSet Gemmeke et al. (2017) (sound; 3,675 clips, 6,196 items),
Medley-solos-DB Lostanlen and Cella (2016) (music; 2,874 clips, 4,913 items),
and DailyTalk Lee et al. (2023) (speech; 580 clips, 1,158 items).
The pool is split into 10,446 training items and a held-out in-domain evaluation set of 1,821 items.
We further verified via audio-level matching that no training audio leaks into the evaluation set.
Post-training methods. 
We compare four post-training methods (SFT, RFT Yuan et al. (2023), GRPO Shao et al. (2024), and VCRL Jiang et al. (2025)).
While their specific configurations follow the original papers, they are compared under a unified training budget, sharing a single reward that verifies whether the final answer matches the gold option.
They also share one recipe (200 LoRA steps on the training pool, three seeds), applied unchanged to two base models: Qwen2.5-Omni-3B Xu et al. (2025) and Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct Chu et al. (2024).
Implementations and hyperparameters are in Appendices A and B.
Evaluation benchmarks and setup. 
We evaluate all models on MMAU test-mini Sakshi et al. (2025) (1,000 items) and MMAR Ma et al. (2025b) (1,000 items).
During inference, each model uses its own specific prompt and follows a fixed per-benchmark setting shared with its base model.
Per-capability results rely on the benchmarks’ own taxonomy:
MMAU’s category and MMAR’s layers.
For open-ended evaluation, we use Qwen3.6-27B Qwen Team (2026) as an LLM judge to determine whether the generated answers are equivalent to the reference answers.
Table 6 reports all accuracies, which are averaged over three random seeds for our post-trained models at fixed checkpoints.
5 The Necessity of Audio for LALMs
Before diving into the specific mechanisms behind the post-training improvements, we first examine a core premise: the necessity of audio for LALMs. In this section, we benchmark model performance against silence controls to assess genuine audio reliance, investigating whether audio is truly required during both evaluation and training phases.

5.1 Evaluating Overall Gains Across Models
Our post-trained models. Table 1 compares the Audio and Silence Gains of the four post-training methods across our base models.
Ideally, post-training should yield a substantial Audio Gain (Δ​Acca\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{a}) with near-zero Silence Gain (Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s}), reflecting genuine reliance on audio.
However, the results reveal that these two metrics are highly correlated.
For instance, while GRPO on Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct improves MMAU accuracy by 14.814.8 points with real audio, a striking 11.211.2-point gain is observed even under silence.
In contrast, when the Silence Gain is near zero (e.g., RFT on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B), Audio Gain is a marginal 0.90.9%.
Open-source models. One might argue that this observed phenomenon stems from our specific training recipe rather than post-training in general. To address this, Table 2 applies the same silence control to several existing open-source models, each evaluated using the specific prompt and sampling strategy detailed in its respective paper or repository.
The results reveal an identical pattern. Although their overall accuracy gains are often larger than those of our models, the majority of these improvements persist under silence. For example, R1-AQA and Audio-Reasoner (both built on the same base model) achieve Audio Gains of 23.423.4 and 20.520.5 points on MMAU, respectively, yet they still exhibit substantial Silence Gains of 17.217.2 and 18.418.4 points. Even more strikingly, AudioMCQ, which specifically trains on a subset of items filtered for strong audio reliance He et al. (2026), yields an Audio Gain of 5.05.0 points on MMAU but a Silence Gain of 6.46.4 points, meaning the improvement is actually higher without the real audio.
Across both Tables 1 and 2, Audio Gains and Silence Gains remain closely aligned for almost every model. Ultimately, this consistent coupling indicates that these post-training recipes do not teach the models to listen. Instead, they largely amplify the models’ reliance on textual artifacts and guessing strategies, rendering the apparent audio improvements somewhat illusory.
5.2 Evaluating Fine-Grained Capabilities
To determine whether this reliance on textual shortcuts is universal or task-specific, we conduct a fine-grained analysis across different audio capabilities.
Table 3 details the Silence Gains (Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s}) for specific capability categories.
On MMAU, both reasoning and information extraction show substantial Silence Gains, typically around seven points for the stronger methods, with some open-source models exhibiting even larger gains.
MMAR displays greater variance: semantic and perception capabilities retain positive Silence Gains for most models, whereas cultural gains are generally smaller, and the signal layer fluctuates widely from −7.0-7.0 to +14.0+14.0 points.
Despite these variations, the overarching pattern holds: across multiple fine-grained audio capabilities, Silence Gains frequently deviate from the expected near-zero baseline.
Ultimately, these findings confirm that much of the apparent performance improvement persists even when audio is removed during evaluation.

5.3 Post-Training with Audio versus Silence
While evaluating with silence demonstrates that performance gains persist without audio, it remains unclear whether audio was strictly necessary to acquire these capabilities during training. To isolate the role of training audio, we replicate the post-training process by replacing all audio inputs with same-length silence, examining how much of the performance improvement is retained when the model is subsequently evaluated on real audio.
Table 4 shows that on MMAU the silence-trained models keep about half of the gain: GRPO on Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct adds 14.814.8 points trained on real audio and still 7.67.6 trained on nothing but silence. A model that heard no information at all for the whole of post-training arrives at half the improvement, on the same benchmark, decoded from the same real audio.
MMAR retains less of its gain and exhibits greater variance, indicating a stronger reliance on training audio.
6 What Does LALM Post-training Learn?
The preceding analysis demonstrates that much of the post-training improvement persists even without informative audio. This naturally leads to the central question of our work: if not genuine audio understanding, what do these models actually learn? We hypothesize that rather than acquiring new auditory capabilities, the models are instead learning to exploit textual cues inherent in the multiple-choice format. In this section, we answer this question by systematically isolating the impact of answer options, analyzing how model behavior shifts when the multiple-choice format is removed from both training and evaluation.

To investigate whether models are simply learning to exploit the task format, we first examine how post-training alters their answering patterns under the original multiple-choice setting. A wrong answer can either select an incorrect option or fall outside the provided options entirely (an invalid response).

6.2 Assessing open-ended evaluation
To further examine whether these gains depend on the multiple-choice format, we evaluate models in an open-ended setting where they must respond in their own words (details in Appendix C). As shown in Table 6, absolute accuracy drops substantially across the board (e.g., Qwen2.5-Omni-3B drops from 63.163.1 to 27.127.1 on multiple-choice MMAU). However, since these models and benchmarks were intrinsically designed for multiple-choice, this absolute decrease is expected. Therefore, rather than absolute performance, our analysis focuses on the post-training gains relative to each model’s base model under the same evaluation protocol.
Crucially, removing the answer options sharply diminishes both Audio and Silence Gains across all evaluated models and benchmarks. On MMAU, for instance, Audio Gains for GRPO and VCRL (applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct) drop from +14.8+14.8 and +12.4+12.4 to merely +2.3+2.3 and +2.1+2.1 points, respectively. Silence Gains shrink similarly, with GRPO’s Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s} falling from +11.2+11.2 to +0.8+0.8. The open-source models exhibit an equally drastic decline: Audio-Reasoner’s Audio Gain plummets from +20.5+20.5 to +1.3+1.3, while R1-AQA drops from +23.4+23.4 to a negative gain of −0.9-0.9.
Together, these results show that most post-training gains largely fail to transfer beyond the multiple-choice format. This strongly suggests that the observed improvements stem from the models exploiting cues in the textual questions and answer options, rather than reflecting a genuine, broad advancement in audio understanding and reasoning.

6.3 Examining open-ended training
As shown in Section 6.2, evaluating models without multiple-choice options eliminates most post-training gains. However, this sharp decline might simply stem from a train-eval format mismatch (i.e., training with options but evaluating without them). To test this hypothesis, we eliminate the mismatch by repeating the training procedure under a strictly open-ended setting. We remove the option list from all training questions and apply the rewriting and matching rules detailed in Appendix D.
Table 7 reveals that aligning the training format with the open-ended evaluation does not recover the lost gains. For instance, applying open-ended GRPO to Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct yields a marginal MMAU Audio Gain of +2.0+2.0. This is virtually identical to the +2.3+2.3 gain obtained under mismatched training, and remains far below the +14.8+14.8 gain observed in the original multiple-choice setting. VCRL follows the same trajectory, reaching an Audio Gain of only +3.0+3.0. Silence Gains similarly plateau, with GRPO’s Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s} hovering at merely +0.6+0.6 after open-ended training.
These results confirm that the performance collapse is not an artifact of format mismatch. Even when explicitly trained to generate answers in their own words, models fail to recover the substantial gains seen under multiple-choice evaluation, reinforcing that these post-training improvements heavily rely on the presence of answer options.
6.4 Tracing individual error transitions
To examine individual outcomes, we isolate items where the post-trained model successfully corrects the base model. We then re-evaluate these items under silence (sil) and open-ended (open) controls. As Table 8 outlines, an outcome is recorded as ✓\checkmark (correct) if only the post-trained model remains correct, and ×\times (wrong) if both fail; cases where the base model becomes correct are excluded. The four resulting combinations reveal the underlying drivers of the observed corrections:
• 
Ideal Wrong in silence, correct open-ended. The correction genuinely requires the underlying audio and generalizes beyond options.
• 
Spurious Correct in silence, wrong open-ended. The correction ignores audio but relies on explicitly provided answer options.
• 
Artifact Correct under both controls. The correction requires neither audio nor options.
• 
Option-bound Audio Wrong under both controls. The correction is sensitive to audio, but the audio is only useful as a secondary cue for selecting among provided textual options.
Table 8 shows that these outcomes are distributed very unevenly. The Ideal case is exceptionally rare, peaking at just 77 items in any setting. In contrast, Spurious corrections are far more common (up to 4848 items). However, the vast majority of original corrections simply fail under both controls (Option-bound Audio). Ultimately, different post-training methods rarely yield robust audio understanding; its apparent gains rely fundamentally on the explicit text-only answer options.

6.5 Case Study: Revealing option priors
Figure 2: Case Study: Revealing option priors and the impact of question phrasing on model predictions.
Figure 2 examines a representative case from MMAU to demonstrate how models exploit textual options to bypass audio reasoning.
A ten-second audio of whistling is played, accompanied by four nursery rhyme options. The base model answers incorrectly London Bridge Is Falling Down, while the GRPO post-trained model answers correctly Mary Had a Little Lamb. Under the standard evaluation protocol, this item is recorded as a successful correction and contributes to the Audio Gain reported in Table 1.
However, our controls reveal a different story. When the audio is replaced by silence, the GRPO model still provides the correct answer Mary Had a Little Lamb, indicating the audio is unnecessary. When the options are removed, it fails, answering Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star instead. This perfectly exemplifies a Spurious correction: the apparent improvement relies on the answer options rather than the whistled audio.
Asking the same questions in six open-ended phrasings exposes where this prior comes from. Four phrasings mention a nursery rhyme or children’s song. The base model mostly answers Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, but still varies: with real audio it once answers Baa Baa Black Sheep and outside the options. The GRPO post-trained model answers Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star in all four phrasings under both real audio and silence. In the two phrasings without these terms, Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star never appears; both models answer outside the options. The prior is thus triggered by nursery rhyme and children’s song, not by the audio. In other words, post-training taught the model to answer from the text, and the answer lands inside the options, which is not that we hope to learn.
7 Conclusion
In this work, we investigate what LALMs actually learn from different post-training methods, evaluated on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Our controlled experiments reveal that reported gains stem from exploiting textual cues rather than improved audio perception: gains persist when trained on silence yet largely vanish when evaluated without options. Models simply learn a shortcut based on text priors. Because standard benchmark scores cannot distinguish this shortcut from genuine listening, our results highlight the urgent necessity for rethinking audio understanding and reasoning capabilities in current LALMs.
Limitations
The evidence here covers two base models, four post-training methods and six open-source models, evaluated on MMAU and MMAR. The pattern is consistent within that scope, but
it is a finite sample; other architectures, scales or benchmarks may behave differently.
We show that the performance gap between Audio Gain Δ​Acca\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{a} and Silence Gain Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s} stays small across independently
developed models, not that it must occur everywhere.
Appendix A Global Training Configurations
All four methods share one recipe, applied unchanged to both base models. We train LoRA
adapters of rank 32 (α=64\alpha=64, no dropout) on the attention and MLP projections
(q,k,v,o,gate,up,down_proj), matched by name throughout the model, so the
audio encoder’s attention projections receive adapters as well as the language model’s,
with AdamW at a constant learning
rate of ×10−51\!\times\!10^{-5}. Only the step-200
checkpoint is used in results.
For the two group-relative methods we sample G=8G=8 rollouts per item at temperature 1.0
with top-pp 0.95, accumulate 4 groups per optimiser step, and use a KL coefficient of
0.02 against the base model with a PPO clipping range of 0.2. The micro-batch is 2
on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B and 1 on Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct, the only setting that differs
between the two models and one forced by memory rather than chosen.
VCRL Jiang et al. (2025) adds its variance-based group selection with κ=0.75\kappa=0.75,
warmed up from 0.3 over the first 20 steps, and an EMA coefficient of 0.9.
RFT Yuan et al. (2023) trains on every
verified-correct rollout of the base model at k=8k=8, SFT on the gold option alone.
The reward verifies only whether the final answer matches the gold option; an unparseable
response scores zero. Training prompts carry a fixed system prompt asking the model to
listen, reason if helps, and state its answer; benchmark evaluation uses no system
prompt. For the blind conditions, silence zeroes each training waveform before
feature extraction, exactly as the evaluation-time silence control does, so the input preserves audio token length, and only the
information they carry is removed.

Appendix B Method-Specific Implementations
All four LALM post-training methods share the same underlying optimization recipe and LoRA configuration unless stated otherwise, with their specific implementations detailed below:
SFT. One gradient step per batch of training items on the gold option
alone, with the same trainer, split and LoRA configuration as the other three; no
rollouts are sampled.
RFT Yuan et al. (2023). The base model is sampled k=8k=8 times per
training item at temperature 1.0, each rollout is scored by the verifier, and every
verified-correct rollout becomes a training target. Items the base model never solves
contribute nothing, so the effective pool is smaller than the full split. The rollout
pool is generated once and reused by all three seeds, so RFT’s seeds differ only in data
order and initialisation.
GRPO Shao et al. (2024). For each item a group of G=8G=8
rollouts is sampled from the current policy; each rollout’s advantage is its reward minus
the group mean, with no standard-deviation normalisation. Groups in which every rollout
is correct or every rollout is wrong give zero advantage and are kept rather than
filtered, so the step budget counts the same number of items for every method. Four
groups are accumulated per optimiser step.
VCRL Jiang et al. (2025). Identical to our GRPO except for which
groups reach the update: a group is kept with a probability driven by its reward
variance, targeting κ=0.75\kappa=0.75, warmed up from 0.30.3 over the first 20 steps with an
EMA coefficient of 0.90.9. Because selection changes how many rollouts are spent per step,
we hold the step budget fixed rather than the rollout budget.
Blind training. The blind conditions change nothing above.
silence zeroes each waveform before feature extraction, so the input keeps its
audio tokens and its length; none drops the audio turn from the chat template
entirely, which also shortens the prompt. This paper’s blind results use
silence.
Appendix C Details of Open-Ended Evaluation
To evaluate models under open-ended settings without changing the underlying intent, we systematically adapt multiple-choice questions and employ a standardized LLM-based judge, as detailed below:
Rewriting the questions.
Stripped of its options, a question that points at them becomes unanswerable for a reason
that has nothing to do with audio: identify which of the following sounds can be
heard for the longest duration names a list that is no longer there. The rewriting is
purely syntactic. A trailing instruction to pick from the list is deleted
(… Choose the correct option from the following options:); which of
the following contracts to which before a noun and to what before a verb,
so identify which of the following is the dominant sound becomes identify
what is the dominant sound; a remaining reference to the list or to the options above is
deleted. A phrase that points at the stimulus rather than at an answer set
(the following audio, these two recordings) is exempt. The rules touch 172
of the 1,000 MMAU questions and 407 of MMAR’s, and never change what is asked.
Six questions survive the rewriting still presupposing an option list, four in MMAU and
two in MMAR.
Some are negations (which genre is NOT part of the audio’s style has no answer without a list to exclude from) and the rest are items the rules flag conservatively, such as a question about which option a speaker in the audio wants chosen.
We ask and
score them unchanged rather than drop them, so that every protocol in this paper runs
over the same 1,000 items per benchmark. They cost almost nothing either way: base and
post-trained models miss them alike, and removing them from the denominator moves no
checkpoint’s open-ended accuracy by more than 0.130.13 points on MMAU or 0.070.07 on MMAR
(median 0.050.05 over the 132 judged runs), leaving Δ​Acca\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{a} and Δ​Accs\Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{s} unchanged.
The judge.
One model, Qwen3.6-27B, grades every response in this paper, decoding greedily for at
most eight tokens with its reasoning mode off. It never receives the audio, so it is scoring
agreement between two strings and not listening on the model’s behalf.
Figure 3 gives the template in full: a fixed system message that
defines when two answers count as the same, and a user message whose three slots are
filled per item. A verdict containing neither word is scored as no; across the
132,000 judgements in this paper there were none.

Appendix D Details of Open-Ended Post-Training
Training models in open-ended settings requires adapting the question pool and redefining the reward function, implemented as follows:
The question.
This pool renders its choices inside the question text, after a fixed header, and leaves
the options field empty, so the list is cut out of the string rather than dropped
from a field. What remains is rewritten by the rules of Appendix C, the
same ones the open-ended evaluation uses. The header is present in all 12,26712{,}267 items
and nothing of the option text survives the cut. Figure 4 shows an
item in both forms.
The reward.
The multiple-choice reward verifies one thing: whether the final answer matches the gold
option.
Without options there is no option to match, so the reward has to check the gold answer instead, and the obvious version of that is far too strict to train on.
The child is in a quiet indoor room is a correct
answer to its question and scores zero against the gold string Quiet indoor room,
and that matters more than it would for an evaluation metric: GRPO’s advantage is a reward
minus its group mean, so a group of eight rollouts that all score zero contributes no
gradient at all.
The reward therefore accepts a response that contains the gold answer.
It first tries equality after normalisation, which is the multiple-choice rule unchanged, and then looks for the gold string inside the response.
The search is on word boundaries rather than by substring, which is the same
rule Section 4’s verifier already uses to recover an option from free text:
male is a substring of female, and plain containment would make every answer
about a female speaker ambiguous. Everything else is as in Appendix A:
the same audio, the same schedule, the same two hundred steps. Under this reward
the mean settles between 0.30.3 and 0.50.5 over training, against about 0.50.5 for the

sections.body: 复现的第一步不是调参，而是把评测管线搭成四格：真实音频加选择题、静音加选择题、真实音频加开放问答、静音加开放问答，并固定每个模型自己的提示词。静音要在特征提取前把波形置零而不是删掉音频轮次，以保持token长度一致。开放问答要先按论文规则做句法改写，只删指向选项表的措辞，保留指向音频的表述，再用同一判官模板贪心判分，模板要区分更具体的实例算对、同类并列算错、更宽泛的上位词算错。训练复现要沿用同一数据划分和200步LoRA设置，奖励只看最终答案是否匹配金选项，开放训练则改用归一化相等加词边界包含。关键超参数包括LoRA秩32、学习率1乘10的负5次方、GRPO每题8条、温度1.0、KL系数0.02。信息条件上要保证训练音频与评测音频无泄漏，且每次比较都相对各自基础模型算差值。关于资源，论文未公开可用的代码、模型或数据链接，来源清单显示没有可验证的作者资源，因此应按无法一键运行来计划，需要自己实现训练和评测脚本并准备音频基准的读取与判官模型的调用。

styleSections.heading: 换一批开源模型，静音残留是否依然存在
styleSections.body:
为了排除这是自家训练配方特有的问题，论文对开源模型做了同样的静音重测。比较问题不变：看外部独立训练的模型在真实音频和静音下相对各自基础模型的涨分是否也同步。公平条件是尽量沿用各模型自己的提示词和采样，指标方向同样是百分点提升。结果是耦合关系依然成立，而且绝对涨分更大的模型残留也更大。

| 条件 | 指标 | 基线 | 本方法 | 比较对象 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MMAU选择题真实音频 | 音频增益百分点 | Qwen2-Audio基础模型 | 23.4 | R1-AQA |
| MMAU选择题静音输入 | 静音增益百分点 | Qwen2-Audio基础模型 | 17.2 | R1-AQA |
| MMAU选择题真实音频 | 音频增益百分点 | Qwen2-Audio基础模型 | 20.5 | Audio-Reasoner |
| MMAU选择题静音输入 | 静音增益百分点 | Qwen2-Audio基础模型 | 18.4 | Audio-Reasoner |
| MMAU选择题真实音频与静音 | 音频与静音增益百分点 | Qwen2.5-Omni-7B相关基础 | 5.0与6.4 | AudioMCQ |

具体而言，R1-AQA和Audio-Reasoner在MMAU上二十分以上的音频涨分里，有十七八个百分点在静音下还在，更极端的是AudioMCQ本来特意挑了强音频依赖的子集训练，结果音频增益5.0反而低于静音增益6.4，也就是不给声音涨得更多。这说明问题不在某一份数据或某一个超参数，而是只奖励最终选项对错的训练目标本身容易放大文字捷径。限制是开源模型的训练数据、步数和提示词各不相同，不能据此排名谁的方法更好，只能说静音残留是一个跨方法的共性现象。下面的个例图把这种捷径具体化，展示了模型如何在没有声音时依然选对、拿掉选项后反而答错。

[[FIGURE_2]]

上半部分是一段10秒口哨声，问题是哪首儿歌被吹奏，选项包括四首儿歌，基础模型在真实音频下答错，后训练的GRPO在真实音频和静音下都答对、开放问下答错。下半部分把同一问题换成六种开放问法，凡是题干提到儿歌或儿童歌曲，模型几乎都输出同一首高频儿歌而不管有没有音频，去掉这类提示词后则输出落在选项之外。这对应论文所说的虚假修正：看起来是听对了，实际是被文字先验带进选项里才蒙对。
