Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
XGEN Team
Abstract
We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer’s audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.
BLOG: https://xgenlabs.ai/research/generative-world-simulation
MODEL: https://huggingface.co/XGENlabs/XGEN-JING
Figure 1: Generative World Simulation. DAO maintains shared world state and updates it in response to actions; JING generates each observer’s first-person audiovisual experience from the resulting conditions. Representative JING trajectories illustrate exploration, object manipulation, character communication, and embodied interaction.
1  Introduction
Video generation models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] have made substantial progress in visual fidelity, motion coherence, and multimodal conditioning, with recent systems also supporting synchronized audio. Their ability to synthesize realistic scenes and dynamic content provides a foundation for generating interactive environments. Building on these advances, interactive world models [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12] generate subsequent observations in response to user or agent inputs, while broadening the range of interactions, extending generation horizons, and improving runtime efficiency. These advances bring us closer to explorable environments that evolve continuously and respond to their inhabitants in real time. They also motivate a further goal: recording and updating world state alongside immediate generative feedback, so that the consequences of actions persist and shape future events and observations. This would connect exploration, manipulation, and communication into a continuous experience grounded in history and shaped by action.
Existing approaches explore different aspects of interactive world modeling. Research on game-based simulation [13, 14, 15, 16] studies action-conditioned generation using gameplay data and virtual environments. Camera-controlled world models [17, 7, 12, 9, 10, 11] enable users to explore generated scenes through viewpoint changes and navigation. Text-controlled world models [8, 18, 19, 20, 21, 11] further allow users to influence character behavior and world events through natural-language instructions. These directions provide increasingly flexible interfaces for interaction within generated environments. An open challenge is to organize the resulting changes into an explicit shared world state that can be queried and updated, evolves according to defined rules, and preserves the consequences of past actions. This becomes particularly important when a world contains multiple actors, evolves over extended periods, or is revisited after an observer leaves. Such a system must maintain shared facts and history while generating each observer’s local experience.
To address this challenge, we present a Generative World Simulation framework comprising DAO and JING. DAO is a computable world engine that maintains the shared world’s state and computes its dynamics. JING is an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model that generates what each observer sees, hears, and experiences next. Actions change the world, and these changes shape the experiences and subsequent choices of humans and agents. This continuous loop connects perception, decision, action, and world evolution within a shared world that persists beyond any individual observer. Users can specify the scenes they explore, the objects they manipulate, and the characters they communicate with, continually influencing both the world and their own experience through interaction. The framework has three core capabilities:
• 
JING: Controllable first-person audiovisual experiences. JING supports flexible combinations of character, object, and scene references, together with observation history and current actions, to generate continuous audiovisual content. Users explore environments through keyboard and mouse inputs and express manipulation and communication intents through text instructions, enabling first-person interaction across diverse settings and visual styles.
• 
DAO: Computable and persistent shared world state. DAO explicitly represents characters, objects, spaces, and their relationships, while maintaining world time and active events. The engine processes actions according to the current state and interaction rules, carries the resulting changes into subsequent states, and retains unchanged information. Past interactions can therefore influence future developments, and world state is preserved as observers change viewpoints, leave, or return.
• 
Continuous closed-loop interaction in a shared world. DAO and JING connect action consequences, local observations, and subsequent choices in an ongoing cycle. Humans and agents act on the audiovisual feedback they receive. The resulting changes enter the shared state and shape future experiences and interaction opportunities. From the same starting context, different choices can lead to different developments, allowing each experience to build on its history while responding to new actions.
We build JING by adapting MiniMax-H3 and training on diverse audiovisual data through a staged pipeline. Bidirectional teacher training introduces camera control, while causal autoregressive training with resampling forcing adapts the model to continuous interaction conditioned on generated histories. Memory adaptation and distillation support the use of historical information and efficient generation, respectively. DAO organizes shared world state through an entity graph, together with actor states, a world clock, and event mechanisms. It updates this state according to spatial constraints and interaction rules, with snapshots and event history supporting persistence. The world state is then converted into observer-specific conditions for JING’s audiovisual generation. This design connects world-state computation with audiovisual experience generation. This report describes the data construction, model training, and world engine design, and examines generation quality, action responsiveness, state persistence, long-term consistency, and runtime efficiency.
Our long-term goal is a persistent shared world in which human and agent interactions have lasting consequences and world evolution continues beyond any individual observer’s presence.
2  Related Work
2.1  Multimodal Video Generation
Video generation has progressed from text- and image-conditioned visual synthesis toward synchronized audiovisual generation with diverse reference conditions. Wan [1] and HunyuanVideo 1.5 [2] advance visual quality, motion coherence, and condition adherence, providing a foundation for generating complex dynamic scenes. Joint audiovisual models, including SyncFlow [22], Sora 2 [3], and LTX-2 [5], model visual and acoustic content together to produce temporally aligned outputs. Seedance 2.0 [4] and MiniMax-H3 [6] further extend multimodal reference conditioning and content control. Together, these advances enable models to represent scene appearance, character behavior, and accompanying sound. Building on this foundation, JING combines character, object, and scene references with observation history and ongoing action inputs to generate continuous, observer-centric interactive experiences.
2.2  Interactive and Egocentric World Models
Interactive world models predict future observations conditioned on actions, extending video generation to environments that users can continuously influence. MineWorld [13], Matrix-Game [14], and Hunyuan-GameCraft [15] learn mappings from player actions to visual feedback in game environments. Matrix-Game 2.0 [17], WorldPlay [7], and AlayaWorld [11] further explore real-time control, streaming generation, and long-horizon interaction. LingBot-World 2.0 [8] and Genie 3 [18] broaden semantic control over character behavior and world events. In egocentric interaction, Hand2World [23] studies gesture-driven object manipulation, EgoSim [24] uses an updatable 3D scene to support continued interaction, and EchoWM [12] combines navigation with video, environmental sound, and speech generation. JING focuses on integrating exploration, manipulation, and communication under flexible reference conditions, allowing these forms of interaction to unfold within a continuous first-person audiovisual experience.
2.3  Long-Horizon Generation and Memory
Long-horizon interaction requires models to use generated history within a bounded computational budget while limiting error accumulation during autoregressive rollouts. Diffusion Forcing [25] and Self Forcing [26] advance autoregressive video modeling through causal generation and training on model-generated histories, respectively. To manage growing context, FramePack [27] compresses historical frame representations, while LongLive [28] combines streaming inference with early-frame retention. WorldMem [16] and WorldPlay [7] improve long-term consistency through history retrieval and geometry-aware memory. OmniForcing [29] extends streaming autoregressive generation to synchronized audiovisual content. For sampling efficiency, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [30] and Velocity Moment Matching (VMM), introduced in EditStream [31], reduce the number of sampling steps through distillation. JING combines adaptation to generated histories, memory utilization, and few-step distillation to support sustained egocentric interaction.
2.4  Persistent World State and Generative Simulation
Explicit state modeling provides queryable and updatable representations of world facts, allowing world evolution to be governed by both state and rules. StatePlay [32] jointly predicts visual content and game states to improve adherence to game mechanics. MASS [33] separates shared-state updates from observation generation: a learned logic engine processes joint actions, and a rendering engine generates observations from the resulting shared state. For spatial and entity state modeling, EgoSim [24] maintains an updatable 3D scene, while Marionette [34] separates structured state prediction, geometric rendering, and appearance synthesis. Programmable World Model [35] further uses executable programs to maintain entity states and transition rules, compiling these states into spatial conditions for video generation. DAO focuses on ongoing character activities and event evolution under explicit interaction rules, translating local world state into observer-specific text, camera, and reference conditions for JING’s first-person audiovisual generation.
3  Data Pipeline
Our data pipeline converts diverse video sources into aligned multimodal training samples for JING. As shown in Figure 2, the pipeline spans data acquisition, source-level filtering, temporal segmentation, captioning, conditioning, and training data organization. Its design emphasizes temporal continuity across navigation, scene revisits, interactions, and dialogue, together with consistent alignment among video, audio, text, and optional camera or reference-image conditions. The following subsections describe the data sources, processing and quality-control procedures, and organization of the resulting training corpus.
Figure 2: Data pipeline overview. Internally collected and generated egocentric videos and open-source datasets undergo automated media checks, model-assisted semantic filtering, temporal segmentation, and captioning. Optional camera trajectories and extracted or generated reference images are aligned with the processed clips and validated before accepted samples are organized by capability and conditioning configuration and packaged into latent representations and LMDB shards for training.
3.1  Data Sources
We construct our training corpus from two complementary sources: internally collected and generated data and open-source datasets. Our data effort centers on egocentric experience: how an environment unfolds from an observer’s first-person perspective as they move through scenes, revisit locations, interact with surrounding entities, and engage in conversations. These experiences guide the selection and construction of our training material.
Internally Collected and Generated Data.
Our internal corpus focuses on egocentric navigation, scene revisits, interaction, and dialogue. We collect first-person videos from a range of publicly accessible platforms, combining broad scene-exploration footage with targeted collections of specific environments and scenarios. These videos capture how scenes unfold as an observer moves through them, encounters nearby entities, and returns to previously observed locations.
We complement this material with game and interactive-video footage acquired through dedicated collection efforts by our team and external partners. These sources expand our coverage of navigation, interactions, and conversations within evolving scenes. We further supplement the corpus with videos rendered in controllable 3D environments and model-generated videos depicting interactions and dialogue, allowing us to construct additional experiences around selected scenes and events. Across these acquisition and generation routes, we prioritize the observer’s first-person perspective and the temporal context of each experience, including continuity across camera movements, scene revisits, and interactions.
Open-source Datasets.
We additionally incorporate publicly released datasets, including SpatialVID [36], Sekai [37], DL3DV [38]. Selected subsets complement our internal collection with additional scene content and camera-motion patterns, broadening the visual and spatial diversity of the training corpus. Together with our targeted collection efforts, these resources provide video material depicting how environments unfold across changing viewpoints and observer movements.
3.2  Processing and Quality Control
Our processing pipeline converts collected videos into training samples with aligned video, audio, captions, and optional conditioning signals. We apply common quality criteria across sources while adapting segmentation and annotation to the temporal structure of navigation, scene revisits, interactions, and dialogue. The objective is to preserve continuous egocentric experiences and provide consistent supervision for training.
Source-level filtering.
We first apply automated checks to media metadata and decoding results, and compute visual-quality metrics on sampled, low-resolution video segments. These checks assess resolution, frame rate, decoding reliability, sharpness, exposure, compression artifacts, and frozen frames. Predefined rules exclude videos with severe defects, while cases requiring contextual interpretation, such as moderate motion blur or potential shot transitions, are retained for further assessment.
Videos that pass this stage undergo semantic assessment using VLM. The model examines frames sampled across the video timeline, short windows sampled at higher frame rates, and available audio to assess first-person perspective, motion continuity, shot transitions, visual overlays, and unrelated background music. The viewpoint criterion requires the camera to represent the observer’s direct experience, without requiring visible hands or other body parts. Motion is evaluated in context: natural walking movements and coherent head turns are acceptable, while unexplained jumps or interruptions that break temporal continuity are grounds for rejection. The model’s structured outputs are checked against predefined acceptance rules to determine whether each source video can proceed to subsequent processing.
Temporal segmentation.
After filtering, we use Qwen3.6 [39] to identify candidate segment boundaries from sampled video frames. These boundaries are adjusted according to the activity being captured. For scene revisits, segmentation aims to keep the departure and return within the same sequence. For interactions and dialogue, it aims to preserve complete operations and conversational exchanges. Each segment retains its source identifier and original time interval, allowing the processed video to be traced back to its source.
Figure 3: Diverse aligned training samples. Illustrative samples covering real-world and virtual-world navigation, scene revisits, object interaction, dialogue, and rendered environments. Within each panel, video frames, captions, audio, and available camera poses follow a common temporal axis, with optional reference images for character, object, or scene conditioning.
Processed clips are packaged into sharded LMDB datasets containing video and audio latents, caption-aligned text embeddings, and applicable camera or reference-image conditions. This unified format supports data from different processing pipelines and enables variants with and without reference-image conditioning to share the same audiovisual content. Each record retains its source, temporal interval, and conditioning settings, preserving alignment and traceability across supervision variants.
Figure 3 illustrates the temporal alignment and optional conditioning of multimodal samples across diverse egocentric experiences.
Video captioning.
We first identify recurring entities and scene context to maintain consistency across segments, then generate captions describing visible events, actions, speech, and relevant sounds. These descriptions are refined into training captions with a first-person perspective. Captions paired with camera trajectories avoid redundant camera-motion descriptions, while those without explicit camera conditioning include the relevant camera movements.
Conditioning and validation.
We construct camera and reference-image conditions for selected samples. For camera conditioning, ViPE [40] estimates camera intrinsics and six-degree-of-freedom poses from processed clips. The resulting trajectories are smoothed and filtered to reduce jitter and exclude unreliable estimates, while maintaining temporal alignment with the video.
Reference images specify characters, objects, or scenes and are obtained by selecting and cropping targets from video frames or generating images from relevant frames and prompts. Each reference is linked to the corresponding caption intervals to align visual conditions with the described content.
Before training, we validate audiovisual synchronization and consistency among media, captions, metadata, and conditioning signals. Automated checks are complemented by inspection of sampled examples, and only samples that pass validation are retained.
3.3  Training Data Organization
After processing and quality control, we organize the accepted data according to the egocentric capabilities they support, including navigation, interaction, and dialogue. Each sample retains its primary capability and relevant secondary attributes, allowing a sequence to capture multiple aspects of an experience. The availability of camera trajectories and reference images further determines the conditioning configurations supported by each sample.
4  Methods
4.1  JING-Experience Model
JING is an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model built on MiniMax-H3 [6] that generates continuous audiovisual content autoregressively. As shown in Figure 4, at generation step kk, the model takes a set of reference images ℛ\mathcal{R}, a text instruction pkp_{k}, camera trajectory 𝐂k\mathbf{C}_{k}, and the previously generated audiovisual history ℋ<k\mathcal{H}_{<k}, and predicts the next video and audio latent chunk:
(𝐙kv,𝐙ka)∼Pθ(⋅∣ℛ,pk,𝐂k,ℋ<k),(\mathbf{Z}_{k}^{v},\mathbf{Z}_{k}^{a})\sim P_{\theta}\!\left(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{R},p_{k},\mathbf{C}_{k},\mathcal{H}_{<k}\right),
(1)
where vv and aa denote video and audio, respectively. The corresponding VAEs decode these latents into synchronized frames and audio, and the generated chunk becomes part of the history for subsequent generation.
Reference images are jointly encoded with text by Qwen3-VL [41] into semantic conditioning tokens 𝐓k\mathbf{T}_{k} and separately encoded by the video VAE into reference tokens 𝐑z\mathbf{R}_{z}, providing semantic conditioning and visual reference information, respectively.
Figure 4: JING architecture. (a) Reference images provide visual conditions through the video VAE encoder and (b) the Qwen3-VL conditioner, which also encodes text instructions. Camera trajectories are processed by a separate control encoder. (c) Current tokens attend to cached keys and values (K/V) from reference and historical context. (d) Camera features modulate video tokens within each Transformer block. (e) Retrieved audiovisual memories supplement the persistent first chunk and recent context. The diffusion sampler produces clean audiovisual latents, which the video and audio VAE decoders convert into synchronized output.
To further support streaming generation, we preserve the temporal order of the latent sequence and reorganize H3’s temporal partition from (5,5,…,2)(5,5,\ldots,2) to (2,5,5,…)(2,5,5,\ldots). The initial 2+52+5 video latent frames form an initialization chunk, followed by chunks of five latent frames each. This layout aligns generation boundaries with the VAE’s overlapping decoding windows, enabling incremental decoding as new chunks become available.
Camera conditions enter the Transformer through a dedicated control encoder. Relative translations and rotations between consecutive camera poses form a six-dimensional motion representation, which the encoder converts into control features 𝐜k\mathbf{c}_{k} aligned with the video tokens in space and time. In Transformer block ℓ\ell, these features modulate the video hidden states through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM):
𝐡~k,vℓ=(1+γℓ​(𝐜k))⊙𝐡k,vℓ+βℓ​(𝐜k),\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{k,v}^{\,\ell}=\left(1+\gamma_{\ell}(\mathbf{c}_{k})\right)\odot\mathbf{h}_{k,v}^{\,\ell}+\beta_{\ell}(\mathbf{c}_{k}),
(2)
where γℓ\gamma_{\ell} and βℓ\beta_{\ell} predict scale and shift, respectively, and ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The modulation acts on camera-conditioned video tokens after the attention residual update and before the subsequent normalization and feed-forward network. Text and audio tokens do not receive this direct modulation, but exchange information with visual features through shared attention. This design introduces camera control while retaining a unified audiovisual backbone.
The attention context for the current chunk combines reference conditions, history at different temporal scales, and the content being generated. After projection into a shared hidden space, its logical composition is
𝐒kτ=[𝐑z;𝐇0;𝐇krecent;𝐌k⏟reference and historical context;𝐓k;𝐙ka,τ;𝐙kv,τ⏟current chunk],\mathbf{S}_{k}^{\tau}=\left[\underbrace{\mathbf{R}_{z};\,\mathbf{H}_{0};\,\mathbf{H}_{k}^{\mathrm{recent}};\,\mathbf{M}_{k}}_{\text{reference and historical context}};\,\underbrace{\mathbf{T}_{k};\,\mathbf{Z}_{k}^{a,\tau};\,\mathbf{Z}_{k}^{v,\tau}}_{\text{current chunk}}\right],
(3)
where τ\tau denotes the noise level during denoising, 𝐇0\mathbf{H}_{0} is the fixed first generated chunk, 𝐇krecent\mathbf{H}_{k}^{\mathrm{recent}} contains the full audiovisual context from recent chunks, and 𝐌k\mathbf{M}_{k} represents memories retrieved from older history. History terms are empty until the corresponding chunks have been generated. Semantic, audio, and video tokens interact through joint attention in the shared Transformer. Attention is joint within each chunk, while access across chunks is causal.
The fixed first chunk provides an initial anchor, recent context supports local continuity, and retrieved memories supply information beyond the current window.
More specifically, JING maintains an audiovisual memory archive to access history beyond the recent window. Retrieval units are video latent frames and contiguous groups of stereo audio latents. After each chunk is generated, the model extracts compact query and key descriptors from the Q/K representations of selected attention layers. At inference time, the query descriptor from the last completed chunk combines information from text and the corresponding modality to score earlier history units:
sk,im=Aggℓ,j⁡(⟨𝐪¯k−1m,ℓ,j,𝐤¯im,ℓ,j⟩dhead),m∈{v,a}.s_{k,i}^{m}=\operatorname{Agg}_{\ell,j}\left(\frac{\left\langle\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{k-1}^{m,\ell,j},\bar{\mathbf{k}}_{i}^{m,\ell,j}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}}\right),\qquad m\in\{v,a\}.
(4)
Here, 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}} and 𝐤¯\bar{\mathbf{k}} denote pooled query and key descriptors, respectively. The indices ii, ℓ\ell, and jj identify historical candidates, attention layers, and attention heads, while dheadd_{\mathrm{head}} denotes the feature dimension of each head. The operator Agg\operatorname{Agg} standardizes candidate scores before aggregating them across heads and layers. The candidate pool excludes the retained first chunk and recent context. Candidates are divided into temporal intervals, and relevant units are selected from each interval to balance relevance with historical coverage. The selected units are replayed through the Transformer with dedicated RoPE position slots and AdaLN memory-role embeddings to obtain memory K/V for the current context. Each newly generated chunk is then added to the archive for future retrieval. By separately limiting the recent window and audiovisual memory budgets, the model bounds the historical context used by current attention while retaining access to earlier experiences.
4.2  JING-Model Training
Using the audiovisual data described in Section 3, we train MiniMax-H3 in five stages to introduce camera control, enable causal generation, incorporate long-term memory, and reduce sampling steps. Together, these stages adapt the pretrained model for continuous, real-time first-person interaction.
We first train a bidirectional teacher with the camera-control module described in Section 4.1. Camera-motion features modulate the Transformer alongside the existing text and visual conditions. We retain bidirectional attention and jointly optimize model parameters and the control module, allowing the model to learn camera-conditioned motion from complete audiovisual clips. This lightweight extension introduces camera control while retaining the pretrained backbone architecture. The resulting model serves as the teacher for subsequent distillation.
We then train a causal autoregressive model to generate audiovisual chunks conditioned on preceding content and current user inputs. We augment teacher-forcing training [42] with resampling forcing [43]: historical segments are perturbed with noise, reconstructed by the model, and reused as context for predicting subsequent content. These reconstructed histories reduce reliance on error-free context and help bridge the gap between clean training histories and model-generated histories at inference. Camera and text conditions can be updated at chunk boundaries, allowing generation to respond to ongoing interaction.
Next, we introduce the audiovisual memory described in Section 4.1 and train the model to combine the fixed initial context, a recent-history window, and retrieved memories. During adaptation, we vary the recent-context length, memory selection, and available memory capacity so that the model learns to use different combinations of historical information. This provides access to earlier scenes and events within a bounded context budget: recent content supports local continuity, while retrieved memories supply cues from beyond the recent window.
To reduce denoising steps, we initialize a few-step student with Velocity Moment Matching (VMM) [31]. VMM matches conditional velocity moments at intermediate noisy states reached during the student’s denoising process. A frozen teacher and a trainable auxiliary network provide velocity estimates that guide the student’s updates. This objective aligns with the backbone’s flow-matching parameterization and supervises states encountered during few-step sampling, providing an initialization for subsequent distribution matching.
Finally, we refine the student with Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [30]. The student generates audiovisual sequences conditioned on its own generated history. A frozen teacher and a score model trained on student-generated samples guide the student’s output distribution toward the teacher’s. Building on VMM initialization, this stage aims to recover quality lost when reducing sampling steps and improve autoregressive generation. The full training pipeline combines camera control, adaptation to imperfect histories, and memory utilization with efficient few-step sampling.
4.3  DAO-World Engine
DAO is a computable world engine that maintains explicit shared state and preserves the consequences of user and agent actions. As shown in Figure 5, a world definition specifies the spatial layout, initial entities, interaction rules, and spatial constraints. State updates are separate from observation readout, allowing different observers to derive their experiences from the same underlying world.
Figure 5: DAO world engine. (a) User and agent actions pass through action admission to produce actor intents and state edits. (b) A world definition initializes a shared state comprising an entity graph, entity attributes, actor states, a clock, and active events. An ordered update cycle transforms WtW_{t} into Wt+1W_{t+1} by applying edits, advancing motion, resolving spatial constraints, and advancing activities, while carrying unchanged state forward. (c) Local readout combines the world state with an observer’s pose to provide observations for an experience interface. (d) World snapshots and event history preserve state across interactions. 
We represent the shared world state at simulation step tt as
Wt=(Gt,Bt,Et,ωt),W_{t}=(G_{t},B_{t},E_{t},\omega_{t}),
(5)
where the entity graph GtG_{t} represents places, characters, and objects through their poses, appearance, semantic attributes, and spatial and attachment relations. Actor and interaction state BtB_{t} records intentions, motion, activities, and attributes such as emotions, needs, and object use. The active event set EtE_{t} represents ongoing events, while the world clock ωt\omega_{t} provides a shared time reference. Together, these components provide a queryable representation of the world for action execution and observation generation.
Inputs first pass through action admission, which resolves targets and checks interaction rules and state constraints, including reachability and target availability. Accepted inputs produce actor intents or queued state edits; inputs that violate these constraints can be rejected. Given admitted inputs 𝒰^t\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{t} and world definition 𝒟\mathcal{D}, state evolution is expressed as
Wt+1=F𝒟​(Wt,𝒰^t),W_{t+1}=F_{\mathcal{D}}(W_{t},\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{t}),
(6)
where F𝒟F_{\mathcal{D}} is the update process determined by the world configuration and rules. Each step applies queued edits, advances actor motion, updates spatial membership and dynamic obstacles, and then advances activities and events. Unchanged state carries forward, so earlier interactions remain part of the world and can affect subsequent actions and observations.

DAO derives local observations from the shared state and observer pose, selecting relevant entities according to sensing range, field of view, and occlusion. These observations provide local entity states, events, and environmental information. Together with camera trajectories and character, object, and scene references, they condition JING’s generation of the next first-person audiovisual experience. Different observers therefore receive local views grounded in the same shared state, and their subsequent actions re-enter the update cycle.
World snapshots and event history support persistence across sessions and process restarts. Snapshots store the state needed to resume simulation, while event history records past interactions. On restoration, DAO reconstructs the world from the saved snapshot and world definition, allowing subsequent actions and observations to reflect the preserved state.
5  Model Performance
We evaluate JING with other video generation and interactive models on WBench [44] and demonstrate its capabilities in reference conditioning, spatial exploration, object manipulation, character communication, branching experiences, and embodied interaction. We further examine DAO’s ability to maintain evolving world states and preserve the consequences of past actions. Together, these results demonstrate XGEN’s capacity to support continuous interactive experiences grounded in a persistent world.
5.1  Quantitative Results
As shown in Table 1, we evaluate JING on the Navigation and Full splits of WBench [44]. Navigation assesses interactive world generation across video quality, setting adherence, interaction adherence, consistency, and physical plausibility. Full additionally covers text-driven subject actions, event editing, and perspective switching, extending evaluation beyond navigation. On the Full evaluation set, our bidirectional and four-step autoregressive (AR) variants achieve average scores of 81.0 and 79.9, ranking first and second among 15 comparison entries. On the Navigation subset, they score 81.9 and 81.0, ranking second and sixth among 39 entries. These results show that our training and distillation pipeline transfers the bidirectional model to a four-step causal generator while largely preserving its overall performance.
5.2  Qualitative Results
Flexible reference conditioning.
Figure 6 illustrates how JING uses different reference combinations to specify the content of an experience. The generated sequences retain recognizable scene features, such as the clock tower and bakery interior, while incorporating the supplied character and object appearances where provided. These examples show how references constrain complementary aspects of generation: the environment to explore, the person to encounter, and the object to interact with.
Figure 6: Reference-conditioned generation. Input references and sampled outputs for three configurations: scene only (a), scene and character (b), and scene, character, and object (c).
Egocentric exploration.
JING translates navigation inputs into changing first-person views across different environments and observer scales (Figure 7). Moving through an archway reveals a street, turning near a shrine exposes surrounding paths, and navigating at beetle scale reveals the space beneath leaves. Nearby surfaces and landmarks remain recognizable across successive views, illustrating local visual continuity as exploration reveals previously unseen content.
Figure 7: Egocentric exploration. Sampled frames from navigation through desert-city alleys (a), a forest shrine (b), and a garden at beetle scale (c). Overlaid controls indicate user inputs during generation.
Object manipulation.
Beyond viewpoint control, JING generates interactions that change nearby objects (Figure 8). The sequences depict tool contact, ignition, and release, linking first-person actions to visible outcomes such as a burning woodpile or an ascending lantern. They illustrate action-conditioned changes in object state and motion across realistic and stylized settings.
Figure 8: Object manipulation. Sampled frames showing a hammer striking heated metal (a), a young dragon igniting a woodpile (b), and hands releasing a sky lantern (c).
Character communication.
JING extends first-person interaction to character communication through generated speech and visual behavior (Figure 9). Across the illustrated languages and visual styles, characters address the observer with changes in gaze, expression, and posture while remaining within the ongoing scene.
Figure 9: Character communication. Sampled frames from conversations in Chinese on a rose terrace (a), English in a fantasy setting (b), and Japanese on a train (c). The corresponding videos include generated speech.
Action-conditioned branching.
Different user inputs can guide distinct continuations from a shared visual context (Figure 10). In the fountain scene, viewpoint control reveals coins in the water, a manipulation instruction produces a coin-toss gesture, and a request to meet a fairy introduces a character encounter. The common opening connects these branches, illustrating how exploration, manipulation, and communication offer different ways to develop the same initial situation.
Figure 10: Action-conditioned branching. A shared fountain opening leads to three continuations: looking into the water (a), tossing a coin (b), and meeting a fairy (c).
Reference-conditioned branching.
Reference selection also shapes how an experience unfolds (Figure 11). Starting from a common bakery opening, the three continuations follow a similar entrance and greeting sequence, but the encountered character changes with the supplied reference. The examples illustrate control over who appears in an interaction while retaining the initial setting and a common interaction structure.
Figure 11: Reference-conditioned branching. A shared bakery opening is paired with character references for Clara (a), Tom (b), and Eli (c), producing different encounters.
Embodied interaction.
Figure 12 presents generated observations from a household robot’s viewpoint. The sequences show manipulators placing a mug, retrieving a ball for a dog, and watering a plant. Successive observations connect these actions to visible changes in nearby objects within a continuing scene. These generated scenarios illustrate a potential observation interface for embodied agents; they do not measure physical robot task success.
Figure 12: Embodied interaction. Generated first-person observations of mug placement (a), ball retrieval for a dog (b), and plant watering (c), viewed from a household robot.
5.3  DAO-World Engine Performance
We evaluate DAO, the world engine of XGEN, through qualitative system demonstrations and ablation experiments, focusing on autonomous agent behavior, first-person views within a shared world, and persistent world-state evolution.
Figure 13: Agents act autonomously and change the world.
Six successive events driven by agent intentions in DAO:
(a) path blocked, (b) intent misread, (c) partial witness,
(d) Clara approaches, (e) evidence checked, and (f) social repair.
Local observations and accumulated evidence guide autonomous actions
from conflict to reconciliation.
Agents autonomously.
Unlike interaction schemes that require explicit user input to trigger events, DAO supports agents that initiate actions autonomously according to the world’s configuration, their own memories, local observations, and available information. Figure 13 illustrates autonomous, intention-driven interaction among DAO agents. Rowan moves a handcart to clear a blocked lane (a), but Eli interprets the displaced parcels as deliberate interference, triggering an argument (b). Nori witnesses part of the event (c), and Clara intervenes on Eli’s behalf (d). Physical traces and witness evidence subsequently clarify Rowan’s intention (e), leading to reconciliation (f). This progression arises from agents pursuing their own intentions and revising their actions in response to local observations and accumulated evidence, while DAO maintains the evolving shared world state.
Figure 14: Different viewpoints of agents in a shared world.
A shared interaction, shown from the
viewpoints of Clara, Eli, and Nori.
One event, different experiences.
DAO supports first-person observations from different agents at the same simulation time, grounding their views of the world and its ongoing interactions in a shared temporal and world-state context. Figure 14 presents the same interaction from the first-person perspectives of Clara, Eli, and Nori. Clara and Eli experience their encounter from opposing viewpoints, while Nori observes it from across the road. DAO derives observer-specific information from a common world state and conditions JING to generate each character’s local visual experience.
Figure 15: JING generation results with and without DAO.
Grounding JING in an evolving world.
DAO provides JING with a persistent, continuously evolving world that maintains an explicit state and supports agents with memory and autonomous, intention-driven behavior. Figure 15 compares JING generations with and without DAO in a departure-and-revisit scenario. Without DAO (top row), the generated revisit depicts the previously ignited napkin as still burning, with no visible evidence of an intervening agent response. With DAO (bottom row), autonomous agent–environment interactions update the world state during the observer’s absence: the attendant extinguishes the fire, and JING conditions the revisit generation on the resulting state. This qualitative comparison illustrates how ongoing world simulation allows actions outside the observer’s field of view to influence subsequent observations, supporting causal continuity across departures and revisits.
6  Conclusion
We present XGEN, a Generative World Simulation framework for sustained human and agent interaction that integrates DAO, a computable world engine, with JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model. DAO maintains and updates shared world state while preserving the consequences of actions; JING generates continuous first-person audiovisual experiences conditioned on references, observation history, and current actions. Together, they connect actions, state updates, and observations in a continuous loop, enabling exploration, object manipulation, and character communication grounded in prior interactions. By coupling world-state evolution with individual experiences, DAO and JING extend audiovisual generation toward simulation of the world behind it. Our long-term goal is the persistent shared world envisioned in OASIS, where encounters carry history, choices have lasting consequences, and social activity continues beyond any individual’s presence. In this vision, humans and agents gain experience and shape a world that evolves through their actions and continues to develop in their absence. Future work will focus on improving motion robustness and long-term memory, reducing response latency, and strengthening consistency between shared world state and generated audiovisual content.

先分清三件事，代码开源、权重可下载、系统可运行是独立的。本篇证据显示作者代码链接当前可用，地址为GitHub上的XGEN-JING仓库，其文档完整性为部分，仅能确认含安装说明；论文提到的Hugging Face上的XGEN-JING页面为第三方链接当前可达；另有研究博客链接本次未能确认可达，WBench榜单页为第三方可达。这些只证明链接可达与论文提到该链接，不证明作者已开源全部训练与DAO实现，来源未确认也不是技术缺陷。

复现第一步建议从推理侧开始，按仓库安装说明核对代码侧内容，先跑JING的单观察者生成，固定场景人物物体参考、文本指令与相机轨迹，验证能否复现钟楼、面包房、马车等参考控制与导航连续，再接入DAO的最小世界定义如Oakhaven小镇、买面包规则与步行遮挡网格，跑通动作准入四步更新局部读出快照恢复的最小闭环。

关键超参数与信息条件要保留，包括分块布局初始化2加5后续每5隐帧、六维相对平移旋转相机表示、只调视频行的特征线性调制、固定首块加最近窗口加检索记忆的预算、五阶段教师重采样记忆速度矩匹配与分布匹配蒸馏的顺序，以及WBench截至2026年9月17日、Full 289例Navigation 158例、Full池15条Navigation池39条的评测条件。训练复现需要自建管线，原文未给出数据规模、采样配比、学习率与算力预算，缺的正是这些项，不要从模型名猜实现。若要验证DAO，至少记录每次状态编辑、拒绝原因、快照与事件历史，并与返回帧一起存档，否则无法区分画面差异来自状态还是采样噪声。

DESIGNING TEXTUAL INTERFACES TO ENHANCE LLM REASONING ON AUDIO-VISUAL QUESTION ANSWERING
Yi Wang
Tianzi Wang
Tong Lei
Dahan Wang
Peter Bell
Abstract
Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers.
We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted.
Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub, with code also being released there 11

Prompt Optimization, Multimodal Reasoning, Omni-modal Large Language Models, Audio-Visual Question Answering, Textual Interface

1 Introduction
Multimodal reasoning requires integrating evidence from multiple modalities to support a decision. In audio-visual question answering (AVQA) task, for example, this may involve identifying relevant evidence from both audio and video, and reasoning over the evidence to answer a question, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
Prior work has improved multimodal reasoning by enhancing chain-of-thought in MLLMs [25, 5],
while another approach is to verbalize multimodal evidence into text for subsequent language-based reasoning, where rich and faithful textual descriptions, combined with additional reasoning by text LLMs, have been shown to improve downstream performance [23, 6, 9, 11].
These findings motivate viewing text as an explicit interface through which multimodal reasoning can be structured and improved.
Recent omni-modal large language models (OmniLLMs), which jointly process audio, video, and text, have achieved strong performance on audio-visual multimodal reasoning tasks [14, 19, 20, 3, 16].
However, their outputs can be sensitive to how the task is instructed. Different prompt instructions for the same audio-visual input may elicit different perceptual details or organize the resulting evidence differently [13, 10], which may make manual prompt design brittle.
Automatic prompt optimization (APO) addresses this problem by using task feedback to iteratively search for refined instructions. Given proper optimization signals and evidence, they usually propose prompt that performs better on downstream tasks than heuristic designs [8, 12, 1].
Figure 1: Demonstration of LLM reasoning on AVQA.
Figure 2: Overview of the three systems we investigated and compared for instruction optimization.
APO methods optimize textual prompts based on text feedback [8, 12, 1]. Recent multimodal APO methods [10, 2] may additionally incorporate multimodal feedback, but the optimized prompts themselves are still represented in text. Therefore, applying APO to a multimodal reasoning system requires the system to expose a textual optimization interface, specifying which textual instructions the optimizer can modify and what feedback or intermediate information is available to guide prompt updates.
The designs of vision-language interfaces for prompt optimization have been studied in previous works [2, 10], but less on omni-modal reasoning over audio-visual information.
To this end, we raise the research question:
does exposing intermediate multimodal reasoning through explicit textual interfaces make APO more effective than optimizing an end-to-end OmniLLM instruction directly?
Thus we explore two types of audio-visual reasoning systems consisting of multi-LLMs, providing different explicit textual optimization interfaces, 1) a captioner-reasoner system that externalizes multimodal evidence into a textual caption before a separate language model produce an answer to the downstream task;
2) an agentic system where a text-based LLM agent raises queries to OmniLLM subagents to collect multimodal evidence for downstream task. And we compare them with the direct inference system, where a single OmniLLM directly consumes multimodal input to conduct the downstream task.
We study these questions through AVQA benchmarks, where a model must answer questions that depend jointly on the auditory and visual streams of a video [26, 21, 7]. AVQA provides a natural testbed because it requires both retrieving sparsely distributed multimodal evidence and reasoning over the retrieved evidence.
Both systems we study are established paradigms for video QA (VQA) or AVQA. Previous works [23, 13, 4] conducted caption-based VQA/AVQA focusing on properly aggregating captions from frames, inducing question-conditioned descriptions, etc. Agentic video systems instead acquire question-relevant evidence iteratively through OmniLLM observation and tool use [17, 24, 18, 15], achieving strong performances. We therefore study captioner-reasoner and agentic systems as representative interfaces for static evidence externalization and dynamic evidence acquisition, respectively.
While prior work primarily designs such systems to improve task performance, we instead study how effectively their intermediate textual interfaces interact with APO, compared with direct OmniLLM inference. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of textual interface design for APO in audio-visual reasoning systems.
Through controlled experiments and error analyses of reasoning trajectories and action traces, we identify distinct limitations in captioner-reasoner and agentic systems, providing insights into further investigation on design and optimization of textual interfaces for audio-visual reasoning.
2 Method
In AVQA, the audio-visual reasoning system aims to predict the correct answer yy, given a video vv with audio aa, a question qq, and answer options oo. This section introduces three system architectures that differ in how audio-visual evidence is exposed through textual interfaces and, consequently, where
textual instructions can be optimized. All LLM parameters are kept frozen. Three systems consist of OmniLLMs and optionally text-only LLMs. In following sections, ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes an OmniLLM and 𝒯\mathcal{T} denotes a text-only LLM, with subscripts indicating their functional roles. ϕ\phi denotes each optimizable prompt, belonging to its corresponding LLM component constructing different systems.
2.1 Direct OmniLLM Inference
We first consider the simplest setting, where an end-to-end (e2e) OmniLLM directly performs AVQA. The model jointly receives the video vv, audio aa, question qq, and answer options oo, and makes prediction y^=ℳe2e​(v,a,q,o,ϕe2e)\hat{y}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{e2e}}(v,a,q,o;\phi_{\mathrm{e2e}}).
ℳe2e\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{e2e}} denotes the OmniLLM used for end-to-end inference and ϕe2e\phi_{\mathrm{e2e}} is its textual task instruction, informing the model that it should conduct the AVQA task and optionally the procedures and rules to follow.
This system exposes the direct-inference textual interface ϕe2e\phi_{\mathrm{e2e}}.
2.2 Captioner-reasoner System
We next consider a two-stage captioner-reasoner system.
The captioner produces
c=ℳcap​(v,a,ϕcap)c=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cap}}(v,a;\phi_{\mathrm{cap}}), without knowing the question and options. ℳcap\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cap}} denotes the OmniLLM captioner, and ϕcap\phi_{\mathrm{cap}} is its textual instruction. A text-only reasoner then predicts
y^=𝒯rea​(q,o,c,ϕrea)\hat{y}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{rea}}(q,o,c;\phi_{\mathrm{rea}}), where 𝒯rea\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{rea}} denotes the reasoning LLM and ϕrea\phi_{\mathrm{rea}} its instruction.
This system exposes two optimizable instructions: the captioner instruction ϕcap\phi_{\mathrm{cap}} and the reasoner instruction
ϕrea\phi_{\mathrm{rea}}.
2.3 Agent-Subagent System
We further consider an agent-subagent system where the text-based LLM agent interactively acquires audio-visual evidence from OmniLLM subagents, and then makes the answer decision.
The primary agent cannot inspect the raw video or directly answer the question without calling a subagent. However, it provides longer context window length not consumed by the large amount of multimodal input, allowing itself to memorize information collected from multiple interaction turns with subagents and reason from such memory.
We adopt one subagent for captioning and another for responding to multimodal evidence-collection queries issued by the text agent. The captioner summarizes globally salient events and provides temporal information about these events, while details omitted from the caption can be further collected through targeted queries, conditioned on the current evidence in captions. These two types of tools are widely adopted in agentic audio and video understanding systems and have demonstrated their effectiveness [15] .
At each interaction step tt, the text agent 𝒯agt\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{agt}} takes an action based on qq, oo, and interaction history hth_{t}.
The workflow always begins with a captioning call to obtain a description of the audio-visual content.
At each subsequent step, 𝒯agt\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{agt}} decides its next action:
zt=𝒯agt​(q,o,ht,ϕagt).z_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{agt}}(q,o,h_{t};\phi_{\mathrm{agt}}).
The action ztz_{t} can be requesting another caption, raising a follow-up query utu_{t} to a query-response component to collect information useful for answering the original question, or producing the final answer once adequate evidence has been collected.
Both the captioning component and the query-response component are OmniLLMs, just playing different roles.
The captioner component is defined as
ct=ℳcap​(v,a,ϕcap)c_{t}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cap}}(v,a;\phi_{\mathrm{cap}}),
and the follow-up query responder component as
rt=ℳresp​(v,a,ut,ϕresp)r_{t}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{resp}}(v,a,u_{t};\phi_{\mathrm{resp}}).
This system exposes multiple textual prompts for optimization, most notably ϕagt\phi_{\mathrm{agt}}. The perception-side prompts ϕcap\phi_{\mathrm{cap}} and ϕresp\phi_{\mathrm{resp}} are also optimizable, and can be adaptively raised by the text agent.
2.4 Automatic Prompt Optimization
During optimization, the system is executed on training examples, whose ground truths are available, using the current instruction ϕ\phi. The optimizer ℱ\mathcal{F}, which is a text-based LLM, observes optimization evidence ee together with the predicted answer y^\hat{y} and ground-truth answer yy, and proposes a revised instruction,
ϕ′=ℱopt​(ϕ,e,y,y^).\phi^{\prime}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}(\phi,e,y,\hat{y}).
(1)
The evidence may include the model response, intermediate reasoning
trajectory, or, for the agent-subagent system, the interaction trace
containing agent actions and subagent observations.
The optimizer iteratively searches over candidate instructions using the training examples. We use QA accuracy as the task-level optimization objective for all APO algorithms. Candidate instructions produced during the search are evaluated on the validation set,
and the instruction with the highest validation accuracy within the specified optimization budget is selected as the final optimized instruction, to be evaluated on the held-out test set.
3 Experiments
We evaluate APO for AVQA on Daily-Omni [26], comparing direct single-MLLM inference, captioner-reasoner pipelines, and agentic system, particularly their compatibilities with an APO algorithm GEPA [1], with brief reference experiment on APO algorithm COPRO [12].
3.1 Evaluation Dataset
We evaluate on Daily-Omni [26], which contains 1,197 audio-visual multiple-choice QA examples spanning six task categories. Since APO requires examples for prompt search and validation-based candidate selection, we stratify the benchmark into 125 training, 125 validation, and 947 held-out test examples,
preserving the overall task-category distribution.
The training set is used during prompt optimization, the validation set for selecting candidate instructions, and the held-out test set as the primary measure of optimization effectiveness. We additionally report full-benchmark accuracy in case for comparison.

4 Results and Analysis
4.1 APO on the Direct-Inference Interface
We first evaluate whether automatic prompt optimization (APO) can improve the direct QA interface of an OmniLLM.
Tables 1 and 2 report the results on Qwen3-Omni and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively.
For Qwen3-Omni, neither COPRO nor GEPA consistently improves direct QA performance. On Qwen3-Omni-Instruct, both optimizers slightly reduce test accuracy relative to the unoptimized prompt.
Qwen3-Omni-Think exhibits a similar pattern: results after executing COPRO and GEPA is comparable with baseline accuracy on the test set, suggesting that exposing a more explicit chain-of-thought reasoning process does not make APO more effective on the direct interface.
In contrast, Gemini-2.5-Flash (abbreviated to Gemini) benefits clearly from GEPA. The test accuracy improves from 75.71%75.71\% to 79.83%79.83\% (by 4.12%), with overall accuracy also showing an increase. COPRO also brings about an accuracy gain of 2.54%2.54\%.
The performance gain obtained by APO on Gemini may be due to the stronger instruction-following capacity of the model, compared to with the Qwen3-Omni models. We therefore primarily use Gemini as the OmniLLM, and GEPA as the APO due to its more stable performance gain across the validation and test splits, in the following case studies on the other two reasoning systems.
4.2 APO on the Captioner-Reasoner Interface
The results of experimenting APO on the captioner-reasoner system are shown in Table 3.
The captioner-reasoner decomposition itself incurs a substantial performance drop compared with direct Gemini inference. Using the same Gemini-generated captions, both Gemini and GPT-4.1 reasoners obtain around 5% accuracy
less than the direct inference. The discrepancy between the reasoner and captioner models did not lead to further accuracy drops.
The drop is possibly because caption forms an information bottleneck between perception and reasoning: the captioner must compress the audio-visual input to text descriptions without knowing which details are key to the question. The downstream reasoner has to make decision on ambiguous observations.
Moreover, providing additional textual interfaces, from only ϕe​2​e\phi_{e2e} to ϕc​a​p\phi_{cap} and ϕr​e​a\phi_{rea}, does not make this architecture easier to optimize. Applying APO to either the caption instruction or the reasoner instruction fails to improve accuracy on the held-out test split. In both cases, validation accuracy increases more strongly than test accuracy. For caption optimization, the validation accuracy rises drastically, while test accuracy decreases from 2.01%2.01\% This large discrepancy suggests that the captioning interface is especially brittle to prompt changes, making it an unreliable target for APO in this setting. Optimizing the reasoner is stable, but does not provide improvement.

4.3 APO on the Agent-subagent Interface
We implemented the agent-subagent system as a ReAct-style pipeline
[22], and applied GEPA. As shown in Table 4, its
performance remains comparable to direct Gemini inference, while
GEPA does not improve held-out accuracy.
To understand the behavior of the agentic interface, we inspect
samples whose correctness changes between direct inference and ReAct.
Among direct-correct but ReAct-wrong cases, the dominant failures are
conflicting perception evidence (61.7%) and incorrect reasoning over
otherwise useful evidence (27.3%). Conversely, ReAct improvements
mainly come from retrieving additional useful evidence or richer
captions. Thus, active evidence acquisition in the agent system can recover missing information, but can also introduce extra failure points.
When applying GEPA on the agentic system, it succeeded in finding an optimized prompt with improved validation accuracy during prompt search, but the improvement does not transfer to test. This discrepancy suggests that the agentic interface is difficult to optimize reliably.
Table 5 further shows that GEPA
acts on different scopes in the two interfaces. The optimized direct
prompt mainly constrains evidence grounding at the final decision,
whereas the optimized ReAct prompt changes a longer chain involving
caption interpretation, query formulation, evidence acquisition, and
integration. Accordingly, GEPA substantially changes the interaction
strategy, reducing the calls to query-responder by 35.8% and total tool calls by 15.0%, yet yielding no gains in held-out accuracy. There are few potential explanations. One is that final-answer correctness alone may provide a weak optimization signal for a multi-stage agentic interface. Or the perception and reasoning ability of the LLM components set limits on how the agentic system can perform.
5 Conclusions
We study whether externalize audio-visual reasoning of OmniLLM-based systems through explicit textual interfaces makes APO more effective than directly optimizing an OmniLLM instruction,which we found is not uniformly the case. APO substantially improves direct Gemini inference, reaching 79.62% overall accuracy on Daily-Omni, despite it not producing much gain on Qwen3-Omni models. In contrast, the captioner-reasoner and agentic systems expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but obtain no reliable improvement from APO. Our error and trajectory analyses reveal interface-specific failure modes, including information loss in captioning, conflicting perception evidence, and downstream reasoning errors. Our results suggest that explicit textual interfaces make multimodal reasoning easier to inspect and steer, but not necessarily make APO more effective.

sections.body: 复现应从直接推理基线开始，因为它是后文所有对照的参照。第一步按论文划分准备Daily-Omni的125训练、125验证、947测试，保持类别分布，分别跑通Qwen3-Omni Instruct、Thinking和Gemini-2.5-Flash的未优化直接推理，核对测试准确率是否落在原表基线附近，再在相同2500次预算下用GEPA和COPRO搜索并做验证选优。关键超参数和信息条件包括优化器大模型固定为GPT-4.1、任务目标固定为问答准确率、模型权重全程冻结、智能体必须先调用描述再决定后续动作、主智能体不能直接看原始视频。代码仓库当前可用，提供了完整优化与推理配置，应优先对照那里的指令模板和评估脚本。权重可下载与系统可运行是两回事：Qwen权重可从第三方页面获取，Gemini需经接口访问，GPT-4.1同样依赖外部服务，只有在这些服务可达且版本一致时才能完整复现智能体与描述者实验。建议记录每次调用的指令文本、交互轨迹和验证测试划分种子，否则无法判断验证提升是否只是选择偏差。

Sankalp Vaish1,
Rishank Singh1,
Sumukh Veeramalla1,
Caroline Summerour2,
John A. Batsis2,
Xiaohui Liang1
Affiliation: 
Affiliation: 1Department of Computer Science,
University of Massachusetts Boston, MA, USA
Affiliation: 2School of Medicine,
University of North Carolina at Chapel hill, NC, USA
Affiliation: 
Email: {Sankalp.Vaish001, Rishank.Singh001, Sumukh.Veeramalla001, Xiaohui.Liang}@umb.edu, 
Caroline_Summerour@med.unc.edu, John.Batsis@unc.edu
September 2025
Abstract
Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models
primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline.
Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall.
We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models.
Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering.
These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.
