I Introduction
Dementia is a growing global health concern, particularly among older adults, and its prevalence continues to increase with aging populations. Early detection is crucial, as timely intervention can significantly improve quality of life and inform effective care planning. Currently, diagnosis is heavily based on standardized clinical assessments, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) [23] is a condition in which people have more memory or thinking problems than other people their age. Individuals with MCI face an elevated risk of progressing to Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias, with studies estimating that approximately one to two out of every ten adults aged 65 or older with MCI develop dementia each year.
Despite the growing success of cognitive impairment [18, 11] detection, most existing studies primarily focus on improving feature representations or fusion strategies, while treating the underlying interaction context as secondary. This leads to a gap in understanding how different tasks influence the quality and discriminative power of behavioral signals.
To address this, there is a need for a systematic, task-centric investigation that explicitly analyzes how different interaction paradigms contribute to cognitive assessment.
In real-world conversational settings, individuals do not produce uniform responses; instead, their speech, language, and behavioral cues vary significantly depending on the cognitive demands imposed by the task. To account for this variability, we design our experimental framework to explicitly model task-dependent behavior. Specifically, instead of treating participant data as homogeneous, we consider three distinct interaction paradigms: Command-Reading (task-1), Command-Generation (task-2), and Question-Answering (task-3), each designed to elicit different cognitive and linguistic processes.
A substantial amount of prior work has focused on speech-based dementia detection, examining acoustic, prosodic, and linguistic biomarkers extracted from conversational speech [4, 7]. Other studies have extended this line of research by incorporating transcript-derived linguistic cues alongside audio features [8]. While these methods demonstrate the utility of speech for cognitive assessment, they largely overlook additional behavioral channels.
To address this limitation, we incorporate visual behavioral cues by analyzing detailed facial emotion patterns [9] and Action Unit [6] derived from video recordings to characterize differences between cognitively healthy and MCI participants.
In this work, we argue that the nature of the collection task itself plays a central role in determining the sensitivity of behavioral signals to early cognitive decline.
We further investigate whether such early signals can be detected through natural facial behavior, speech, and language use. In addition, we analyze how these behavioral cues vary across tasks, providing insight into which interaction paradigm is most informative.
Beyond facial cues, we extract audio biomarkers and textual linguistic features, building on prior speech-driven dementia studies [4]. Each modality is first evaluated independently, followed by integration within a unified multimodal framework to assess the benefits of fusion over individual signals. Our findings show that such multimodal models can detect early cognitive impairment even from short, casual interactions.
This work makes the following key contributions:
1. 
A conversational dataset with structured interaction tasks.
We created a dataset collected across multiple sessions through three distinct Alexa-based tasks. Unlike traditional clinical datasets, these tasks are designed to capture diverse cognitive behaviors, including natural conversation, semi-structured interaction, and memory-based question answering. This diversity enables the analysis of task-specific cognitive signals, providing a more realistic setting for home-based screening.
2. 
Unified multimodal preprocessing pipeline:
We develop an end-to-end pipeline for extracting standardized features across all three modalities, including (i) facial Action Units and frame-level emotion probabilities from video, (ii) acoustic and prosodic biomarkers from participant speech, and (iii) linguistic, semantic, and cognitive-linguistic features from transcripts. These then act as a input to transformer encoder architecture with multi-head self-attention to capture time-series data.
3. 
Task-level analysis:
We observe that unimodal models are highly task-sensitive across the three interaction paradigms. The video model performs better on task-1 and task-2, achieving an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69) on Task 1, but degrades on Task 3, where it attains an accuracy of 0.59 (AUC 0.59). In contrast, the audio-based model performs best on task-2 and task-3, reaching its highest performance on task-3 with an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73).
4. 
Comprehensive evaluation of unimodal and multimodal models:
We treat each task as a distinct data point and observe consistent trends across modalities. The video model produces a higher number of Type I errors (41) compared to Type II errors (22), whereas the audio model exhibits the opposite behavior, with more Type II errors (46) than Type I errors (14). In contrast, the multimodal model reduces both error types to 21 (Type I) and 16 (Type II),
indicating that multimodal fusion effectively leverages complementary predictive strengths of different modalities.
II Related Work
Early detection of dementia traditionally relies on standardized clinical assessments, which require trained examiners and controlled environments, limiting scalability and frequency of testing. As a result, automated and contactless approaches have gained significant attention.
Facial behavior, like emotional expressions and action units, offers another rich modality for cognitive health analysis. Prior studies have demonstrated that facial expressions may help differentiate individuals with dementia from healthy controls [9]. However, such work typically treats facial cues as a stand-alone modality, without integrating them with speech or linguistic features. To date, no existing study has combined audio, text, and video into a unified multimodal framework for dementia detection, despite increasing evidence that cognitive decline manifests across all three domains.
Recent advances in affective computing and sentiment analysis further highlight the value of multimodal behavioral cues in machine learning systems [22, 3].
Building on this, Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly emerged in healthcare applications, supporting clinical decision-making, diagnostics, and multimodal reasoning. These systems leverage domain-specific pretraining, fine-tuning, and prompt engineering techniques to interpret diverse data types [14]. Despite this progress, the potential of LLMs to reason over multimodal behavioral biomarkers for cognitive impairment remains largely unexplored.
Some research has also incorporated neuroimaging modalities such as MRI and PET scans for dementia diagnosis [2, 12]. Although effective, these methods are costly, inaccessible, and unsuitable for home-based or longitudinal monitoring. In contrast, behavioral signals from everyday interactions (speech, facial expressions, and language) offer a scalable alternative that can be captured unobtrusively through common consumer devices.
A recent study, Cog-TiPRO [15], demonstrated the feasibility of using voice-assistant-based speech and linguistic data for longitudinal detection of cognitive decline [cite]. However, that work, like most prior research [13, 11], omits video-derived behavioral cues. Our work advances this direction in three important ways: (1) by adding facial expression and Action Unit analysis, capturing non-verbal indicators that may manifest earlier than speech changes; (2) by combining video, audio, and text in a unified multimodal pipeline; and (3) by evaluating across multiple structured interaction types and sessions, enabling a more comprehensive and ecologically valid evaluation for real-world, home-based screening.
III Methodology
III-A Preprocessing
Fig. 1: Processing Pipeline
The dataset consisted of synchronized audio–video recordings of participant interactions with Alexa, complemented by automatic transcripts generated via Rev.ai. All three modalities were preprocessed to extract meaningful behavioral features before their integration into the unimodal and multimodal models. Figure 1 illustrates the pipeline from raw recordings to modality specific feature embeddings and
their mapping to various modeling architectures.
Video Encoder:
To address the presence of multiple individuals in each recording (participant, interviewer, Alexa device, questionnaire holder), we first applied MiVOLO [10] to every frame for face detection and age estimation. This allowed us to isolate the older adult participant across all sessions.
Emotion Features: We employed ResEmoteNet [19], to estimate frame-level emotional states (happy, sad, angry, surprise, neutral, disgust, fear). For each speaking segment, we aggregated these predictions into quantitative descriptors [9], including:
emotion counts, emotion distribution, emotion variability, and frequency of emotion shifts.
Action Unit Features:
To capture more granular facial behavior, we used OpenFace [1]
to extract Facial Action Units (AUs), which quantify the activation of specific facial muscles (e.g., AU1: Inner Brow Raise, AU12: Lip Corner Pull). These AUs provide a physiologically grounded representation of subtle facial movements  [6] that may correlate with cognitive decline.
Audio Encoder
Using Parselmouth and Librosa, we analyzed only the participant’s speech segments [18, 5]. Two families of features were extracted:
Acoustic Features: MFCC statistics, Spectral centroid, Spectral flux, Harmonics-to-noise ratio.
Prosodic and Speech Biomarkers: Pitch (F0) metrics, Intensity contours, Jitter and shimmer, Speaking rate, Pause and Articulation rate.
Text Encoder:
Transcripts generated by Rev.ai were processed using NLTK, TextBlob, and Sentence Transformers [24, 17],
to derive these features:
Linguistic and Semantic Features: Lexical richness, Syntactic complexity, Semantic coherence, Use of filler words, hesitations, and discourse markers.
Semantic Embeddings
Sentence-level embeddings were extracted using a Sentence Transformer model, followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to retain the top 10 components representing the semantic structure of speech.
III-B Modeling
Our modeling framework systematically evaluates the contribution of different tasks using a diverse set of models, ranging from traditional machine learning classifiers to multimodal transformer architectures that capture temporal dynamics in the extracted features from the above-described pipeline. We use a standard transformer encoder architecture with multi-head self-attention for sequence modeling [16], [21, 20].
We first trained separate models on each of the three tasks to identify which task provides the most informative signals for dementia detection. We then evaluated unimodal models for each task and compared their performance with a multimodal model that integrates information across tasks and modalities, enabling us to isolate the cognitive and behavioral cues.
IV Dataset
The dataset was collected from 35 older adult participants through a series of structured interactions with Amazon Alexa. Each experimental session was divided into three distinct tasks, designed to elicit different forms of verbal
engagement:
Command-Reading (task-1): Participants were provided with a list of 30 predefined questions (e.g., “What is the weather outside?”, “What is today’s date?”) and instructed to ask Alexa directly. This task primarily assessed verbal clarity and recall when following straightforward instructions.
Command-Generation (task-2): Participants were given 30 intent prompts (e.g., weather, date, news) and asked to independently formulate appropriate questions to pose to Alexa. This task introduced a higher cognitive load, evaluating language generation, flexibility, and planning. Question-Answering (task-3): Alexa presented participants with 30 pre-recorded questions (e.g., “Name some animals you would find in a zoo”), and participants were required to respond verbally. This task targeted comprehension, memory recall, and spontaneous speech production.
Fig. 2: Data
Figure 2 provides an overview of the dataset structure, illustrating the duration and composition of each experimental session. One session lasted approximately 35–75 minutes and included all three tasks and was repeated 7 times over a period of 18 months. The figure also displays the MoCA score serves as the primary ground-truth labels for cognitive status estimation. Participants with MoCA scores between 18 and 25 were categorized as having Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), while those scoring 26 or above were considered cognitively healthy.
Finally, the figure lists all participant IDs and their corresponding session numbers. No personal or identifiable information is included, ensuring full anonymity and compliance with privacy standards.
V Results
V-A Emotion Analysis
Fig. 3: Relationship between Emotion Count and Emotion
Figure 3 presents a boxplot illustrating the distribution of emotion counts across participants. The results indicate that individuals in the healthy group (orange) exhibit a higher frequency of positive emotions, such as happy and neutral, whereas participants with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) (blue) display a greater occurrence of negative emotions, including sadness, disgust, and surprise. This trend suggests that emotional expressivity and valence patterns may serve as behavioral indicators of cognitive decline.
Fig. 4: Emotions’ distribution for a MCI Participant
Figure 4 illustrates emotion variation across tasks for a participant with MCI. Negative affect, particularly sadness (blue), is prevalent across tasks, while happiness (orange) appears infrequently, suggesting reduced emotional variability and diminished positive affect. Notably, task 3 shows a marked increase in sadness, likely corresponding to moments when the participant was searching for or formulating an answer, potentially reflecting increased cognitive effort or task-related frustration. Overall, the emotional profile appears more constrained and skewed toward negative affect.
Fig. 5: Emotions’ distribution for a healthy Participant
In contrast, Figure 5 shows emotion variation for a cognitively healthy participant, where positive emotions, especially happiness, are more consistently expressed across tasks. This predominance of positive affect, along with broader emotional variability, may reflect stronger emotional regulation and preserved cognitive functioning. Even during more cognitively demanding tasks, the participant maintained positive emotional expression. In particular, task 3 exhibits richer emotional variation compared to the MCI participant, suggesting greater affective flexibility in response to task demands.
Task 1 shows a notable difference in how each participant initially perceives and engages with the task. As task complexity increases across tasks, the participant with MCI exhibits reduced emotional expressiveness and diminished variability in affective responses, whereas the healthy participant maintains richer emotional expression.
V-B Audio Analysis
Fig. 6: Audio Features Distributions by Cognitive Status
The figure 6 illustrates the normalized distributions of key acoustic features for speakers with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and cognitively healthy controls. Individuals with MCI show lower pitch variability, reduced speaking and articulation rates, and longer pauses, indicating less dynamic prosody and slower, more effortful speech production. Measures of voice stability (jitter, shimmer, HNR) also suggest less stable phonation in the MCI group. Together, these patterns highlight consistent differences across prosodic, temporal, and voice-quality features, supporting their potential relevance as markers of early cognitive decline.
Fig. 7: Audio Feature distribution for a MCI Participant
Figure 7 illustrates the distribution of some normalized acoustic features across sessions, enabling comparison of different tasks for participant VASP2015 with MCI. In task-1, the participant exhibits elevated pitch measures and moderate vocal instability, suggesting increased cognitive load during task initiation. Further, task-2 reveals a partial normalization of pitch but continued irregularity in temporal features such as speaking rate and articulation rate, indicating difficulty maintaining consistent speech rhythm during sustained interaction. By task-3, pitch variability increases again and hesitation markers, including pauses become more pronounced, maybe because of potential fatigue or diminished cognitive control as the tasks progress.
Fig. 8: Audio Feature distribution for a healthy Participant
Figure 8 displays the same acoustic features for Participant VASP2024, a cognitively healthy control. This participant exhibits more compact and consistent distributions across nearly all measures. Task-1 shows controlled pitch values and balanced pause behavior, consistent with efficient task engagement from the outset. Task-2 maintains this stability, with articulation and speaking rates remaining tightly clustered and voice-quality measures (jitter, shimmer, HNR) indicating sustained phonatory control. Task-3 introduces more expressive variation such as slightly increased pause frequency and wider pitch range, but these shifts remain within the bounds of healthy adaptive modulation rather than cognitive strain.
Utterance duration during task 3 suggests that this task elicits longer verbal responses for both groups. However, the healthy participant exhibits more sustained and consistently longer utterances, particularly in task 3, with tighter distributions indicating more stable response patterns. In contrast, the cognitively impaired participant shows greater variability in utterance duration, especially in the later task, suggesting less consistent speech production.
The cognitively impaired participant (VASP2015) generally exhibits higher variability in jitter and shimmer, particularly in tasks 2 and 3. Since jitter captures cycle-to-cycle frequency instability and shimmer reflects amplitude instability, elevated or more dispersed values may indicate less stable phonation and greater vocal irregularity.
In contrast, VASP2024 exhibits controlled, stable, and predictable acoustic behavior across sessions. The contrast between the two distributions supports evidence that MCI is associated with increased acoustic variability, disrupted speech timing, and reduced vocal stability, highlighting the potential of speech-based measures as sensitive indicators for early cognitive decline. Moreover, the MCI participant displays task-dependent destabilization, with greater variability and performance decline from task-1 to task-3, while the healthy participant maintains consistent control with slight changes.
V-C Model Analysis
Fig. 9: Comparison of Accuracy and AUC across tasks
Figure  9 presents a comparative analysis of four models across three experimental tasks. The plot displays Accuracy (solid lines with circular, diamond, and triangular markers) and AUC (dashed lines with square, plus, and inverted triangle markers) for each task.
The Video model performs particularly well on task-1 and task-2, suggesting that these tasks provide richer and more discriminative facial expressions associated with cognitive state. In contrast, the Audio model achieves stronger performance on task-3, indicating that question answering better exposes verbal inconsistencies and speech-based cognitive markers.
Notably, the Video + Audio + Text model demonstrates the most consistent performance across all tasks, maintaining relatively stable Accuracy and AUC values.
Across models, tasks 2 and 3 consistently provide more informative signals, reflected in higher Accuracy and AUC scores, whereas task-1 appears comparatively less discriminative, exhibiting slightly lower performance and greater variability.
Fig. 10: Comparison across different models
Figure 10 illustrates how classification errors evolve as additional modalities are incorporated (0 = MCI). For this analysis, each task was treated as an independent data point, enabling an across-task rather than within-task analysis. This allows the model to capture variations in behavioral and emotional patterns across different tasks. The unimodal models exhibit a tendency toward dominant-class bias, leading to asymmetric misclassification patterns.
The Video Model provides a baseline performance, correctly identifying 36 MCI participants, but suffers from substantial false negatives, misclassifying 41 healthy participants as MCI, indicating limited discriminative capability when relying on visual emotional cues alone. The Audio Model improves class separation by reducing false negatives from 41 to 14 and substantially increasing correct healthy classifications (72), though it introduces a high number of false positives for the MCI class, suggesting a bias toward predicting healthy controls.
The combined Video+Audio+Text model achieves the most balanced and reliable detection, correctly identifying 37 MCI participants while reducing overall misclassifications to 16 false negatives and 21 false positives, demonstrating that integrating complementary behavioral signals mitigates dominant-class bias and improves class separability.
VI Discussion
The findings of this study demonstrate that natural conversational behavior contains meaningful signals for the early detection of cognitive impairment. Facial emotion patterns and AU dynamics reveal clear distinctions between cognitively healthy and MCI participants, with the latter exhibiting a higher prevalence of negative affect and reduced emotional variability. In addition, audio-based biomarkers and linguistic features provide complementary indicators of impairment, capturing disruptions in prosody, speech fluency, and semantic coherence. Together, these results highlight the importance of integrating visual, acoustic, and linguistic cues to obtain a more comprehensive characterization of early cognitive decline in naturalistic interaction settings.
Task-wise comparisons showed that tasks requiring question-generation or spontaneous responses produced more informative video signals while predefined question answering gives more informative audio signals.
Looking ahead, several directions can strengthen and extend this work. Expanding the dataset with more participants and diverse demographics will improve generalizability.
We will also focus on longitudinal and cross-session modeling using Transformer-based sequence models to capture subtle behavioral changes across sessions.
Additionally, we will focus on improving multimodal fusion strategies and exploring LLMs to provide more interpretable and clinically meaningful reasoning over behavioral signals.
VII Conclusion
This work introduces a multimodal preprocessing pipeline that integrates facial behavior, audio biomarkers, and linguistic features to distinguish cognitively healthy individuals from those with MCI.
In contrast to traditional models our framework leverages the inherently multimodal nature of human communication to capture a richer and more comprehensive representation of cognitive function.
By analyzing emotional dynamics, we show that meaningful cognitive signals emerge even during casual conversational tasks, with Command-Reading and Command-Generation revealing richer behavioral markers than structured question-answering tasks. Moreover, acoustic and linguistic cues provide complementary information, particularly in tasks such as Command-Generation and Question-Answering, highlighting the value of modeling task-dependent multimodal behavior across tasks.
Our results demonstrate that combining all three modalities substantially improves predictive performance (accuracy = 0.75, AUC = 0.80), outperforming any unimodal system.
This approach enables scalable, continuous monitoring through natural interactions without clinical instrumentation, reflecting a real-world environment.
This framework can be embedded into telehealth workflows, smart-home devices, video-calling platforms, and digital wellness applications, enabling continuous, remote monitoring and early alerts for cognitive decline.
VIII Acknowledgement
This research was funded by the US National Institutes of Health National Institute on Aging R01AG067416.

sections.body: 数据集来自35名老年被试的结构化Alexa交互，每次会话包含全部三个任务并重复7次，时间跨度18个月，单次约35至75分钟。论文图2展示了被试编号、MoCA分数、年龄、性别、婚姻和分钟数等结构，例如示例行里VASP2001到VASP2007的MoCA均值在22.57至29.42之间，年龄68至74岁，单次分钟数约35.94至46.14分钟，说明样本是小样本纵向设计。标签以MoCA分数为准，18至25为轻度认知障碍，26及以上为健康，不含可识别个人信息。评测指标用准确率和曲线下面积，准确率越高越好，曲线下面积越接近1越好，0.5接近随机猜测。任务级分析把每个任务单独评测，跨任务分析则把每个任务当作独立数据点，看行为和情绪模式跨任务的变化。论文结论报告的三模态总体准确率0.75和曲线下面积0.80属于跨任务聚合结果，与分任务单独评测的准确率和曲线下面积来自不同聚合方式，不直接相减得到提升幅度。需要提醒的是，35人乘多次会话再乘三个任务，样本量在任务级会被放大，但被试数本身很小，不同会话来自同一人，独立性有限，结论成立的前提是这种划分不泄露被试信息，而原文没有交代被试无关划分，这是解读时必须保留的限制。

sections.heading: 哪个任务对哪个模态更友好，多模态是否更稳
sections.body:
下面这张表回答论文第一个核心问题：任务和模态是否匹配。比较条件是同一批Alexa交互按任务拆开评测，指标是准确率和曲线下面积，都是越高越好。这里比较的是任务内单模态和融合模型的相对优劣，不是跨数据集的绝对排名，任务一偏朗读复述，任务二偏生成组织，任务三偏即兴问答，信号类型本来就不同。

| 条件 | 指标 | 视频模型 | 音频模型 | 三模态融合模型 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 指令朗读任务一 | 准确率 | 0.65 | 未报告 | 0.76 |
| 指令朗读任务一 | 曲线下面积 | 0.69 | 未报告 | 0.75 |
| 问答任务三 | 准确率 | 0.59 | 0.67 | 0.76 |
| 问答任务三 | 曲线下面积 | 0.59 | 0.73 | 0.73 |

这张表比较的是分任务下的相对表现，结果要在任务信号差异的条件下理解。视频模型在任务一0.65准确率和0.69曲线下面积是它的最好成绩，到任务三掉到0.59和0.59，说明预设朗读里的面部表情更具判别力，而问答时面部信号变弱；音频模型在任务三达到0.67和0.73，是它的最高点，说明问答更能暴露言语不一致和语音认知标记；三模态在任务一0.76和0.75、在任务三0.76和0.73，跨任务最稳。论文结论还报告三模态总体准确率0.75和曲线下面积0.80，超过任何单模态，但该总体数和分任务数来自不同聚合方式，不能直接相减得到提升幅度。未胜出项是任务一对音频并不友好，任务三对视频明显退化，说明单模态高度任务敏感，这是融合的动机而非单模态无用。

Hierarchical Interpretable Multitask Audio Representation Learning: An Analysis of Event–Scene Relationships through the Information Bottleneck
Claudia Montero-Ramírez
Alba Martínez-Serrano
Carmen Peláez-Moreno
††thanks: ††thanks: Manuscript received October 2026
Abstract
Joint Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) and Audio Tagging (AT) models traditionally rely on unconstrained multihead architectures. However, this design ignores the natural hierarchical dependency between sounds and acoustic scenes. In this work, we investigate a hierarchical (sequential) conditioning paradigm that predicts scene categories directly from intermediate event probabilities. Through a large-scale empirical benchmark with 66 full training runs across three state-of-the-art backbones (PaSST, PANNs, and BEATs) and different loss-weighting settings (β∈[0.0,1.0]\beta\in[0.0,1.0]), we show that hierarchical conditioning achieves competitive classification performance while altering multitask optimization dynamics. Unlike multihead baselines, which sequentially solve the easier ASC task before optimizing AT, the hierarchical architecture enables synchronized dual-task learning for specific loss-weighting settings (β∈[0.6,0.9]\beta\in[0.6,0.9]). Furthermore, we propose a multi-perspective interpretability framework that combines an analysis of the information bottleneck, manifold geometry, and Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) on a Term-Frequency Inverse-Document-Frequency (TF-IDF) event representation, providing complementary insights into event–scene relationships.
Our findings reveal that hierarchical conditioning systematically yields lower conditional entropy, higher mutual information, and superior latent cluster separability (higher Silhouette scores), establishing a more structured and semantically faithful intermediate feature space.
Index Terms: Acoustic Scene Classification, Audio Tagging, Multitask Learning, Hierarchical Conditioning, Information Bottleneck, Formal Concept Analysis, Representation Interpretability.
I Introduction
Sounds are the fundamental component of an acoustic scene. A group of sounds can define an acoustic scene for human understanding. E.g., if we close our eyes and listen to a bird singing, the sound of a waterfall, and the leaves on the trees rustling in the wind, we will surely find ourselves in an outdoor scene, surrounded by nature.
However, an acoustic scene is rarely defined solely by the isolated sound events occurring within it; rather, human auditory perception relies on both discrete acoustic events and a continuous, ambient background texture—frequently referred to as the acoustic ”gist” [1]. In other words, while discrete events (such as footsteps or a dog barking) provide solid semantic reference points, the underlying acoustic gist captures the spatial reverberation and diffuse background noise that characterize the environment globally.
Replicating this ability computationally has become an increasingly important research goal with the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI). We have known for years that machines can hear—ever since we became capable of recording audio. However, advances in AI have progressively enabled machines to move beyond simply capturing sound towards interpreting what is happening within audio recordings [2]. Along with this paradigm, research communities such as DCASE [3] have emerged, launching annual challenges to bring together scientists from around the world to share knowledge in these areas. One of the tasks they propose is Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) [4], which aims to automatically identify the location where the audio was recorded. They also offer tasks such as Audio Tagging (AT) [5], which aims to identify which sounds are present in each audio clip, and Sound Event Detection (SED) [6], which works in the same way but with the added capability of identifying the specific time points at which those sounds occur. In this work, we focus on AT rather than SED, as our interest lies in the global set of acoustic events that characterize a scene rather than in their temporal occurrence.
A key challenge in studying event-scene relationships is the limited availability of datasets providing both scene and sound event annotations. We therefore focus on TUT
Sound Events 2016/2017 [7] and TUT Acoustic Scenes 2016 [8] and evaluate three pretrained audio backbones— Patchout faSt Spectrogram Transformer (PaSST), Large-Scale Pretrained Audio Neural Networks for Audio Pattern Recognition (PANNs), and Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Audio Transformer (BEATs) — to assess the consistency of our findings across different acoustic representations.
However, going back in time, it was very common to use hand-crafted features as input for models to solve these tasks. These representations included features such as MFCCs, pitch, and the energy of the audio signal, and they enabled predictions to be interpretable. E.g., audio with sustained high energy over time is more likely to come from a noisy place than a quiet one. Over time, AI has become more sophisticated, giving rise to what we call “black boxes”: Deep Learning Networks (DLNs). Alongside them—and more recently—have come transformers, a type of architecture that has become absolutely dominant in data-rich settings.
These models achieve fantastic metrics and typically use the spectrogram image as an input feature. However, they are called “black boxes” because, due to their large number of parameters, we lose track of what is happening inside the model from the perspective of interpretability. Nevertheless, techniques have been developed to understand parts of these models, such as SHAP [9], LIME [10], and the information bottleneck theory [11], proposed by Naftali Tishby.
Beyond understanding what information is used by a model to make a prediction, an additional question arises when several related aspects of the same audio signal are considered: which information is shared across tasks, and which information is specific to each one? This question becomes particularly relevant for acoustic scene understanding, where the environment and the sounds occurring within it are intrinsically related.
A promising strategy for exploiting these relationships is multitask learning. In this paradigm, a single model is trained to perform several tasks simultaneously, sharing part of its internal representations. The idea is that related tasks can benefit from one another, since the information learned in one task acts as an inductive bias for the others. In the context of audio, this allows a model to simultaneously learn to classify acoustic scenes (ASC) and detect sounds or events (AT/SED) using a shared backbone that extracts general representations from the audio data.
After the backbone, multihead layers are added so that there are small, specialized models for each task, as shown in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1: a) Traditional architecture of multitask models with multiple heads [12, 13, 14]. b) Our proposed hierarchical architecture using an information bottleneck with a feed-forward network (FFN).
Most existing multitask audio models adopt a multihead architecture, in which task-specific prediction heads operate on a shared representation learned by a common backbone. While this design enables the joint learning of related tasks such as ASC and AT, it does not explicitly constrain how information about acoustic events contributes to the representation used for scene prediction. This raises an important question: how are event-level acoustic concepts preserved and organized when learning to predict the scene, and how does this organization depend on the architecture used for multitask learning?
Despite the growing interest in multitask audio representation learning, most existing approaches focus primarily on predictive performance, while comparatively little attention has been devoted to understanding how acoustic event information is organized within representations that also support scene prediction. In particular, it remains unclear which event information is preserved, how strongly it is associated with the predicted scene, and whether different multitask architectures induce different event-scene relationships. Addressing these questions requires going beyond classification performance and examining the learned representations themselves.
This motivates us to introduce a hierarchical architecture in which the intermediate event representation directly conditions the scene prediction. Rather than treating event and scene predictions as parallel outputs of a shared representation, this formulation explicitly models the event-to-scene dependency and introduces a well-defined intermediate bottleneck through which this relationship can be examined (Fig. 1). The resulting architecture therefore provides not only an alternative way of performing joint ASC and AT, but also a natural framework for studying how event information is preserved and transformed when predicting acoustic scenes.
The main objective of this work is therefore to investigate how the choice of multitask architecture affects the relationship between acoustic events and acoustic scenes in pretrained audio models. To this end, we compare conventional multihead multitask learning with a hierarchical architecture that uses the intermediate event representation to predict the acoustic scene.
More specifically, this work aims to:
1. 
Evaluate the hierarchical and multihead architectures across different pretrained audio backbones and task-loss weights, analyzing their effect on ASC and AT performance.
2. 
Characterize the event representations learned by both architectures using information-theoretic and geometric measures, including conditional entropy, mutual information, KL divergence, and clustering quality.
3. 
Analyze how the learned event representations preserve the semantic relationships between events and scenes, using Term-Frequency Inverse-Document-Frequency (TF-IDF) weighting and Formal Concept Analysis (FCA).
4. 
Assess whether the explicit event-to-scene bottleneck provides a more transparent representation of event-scene relationships than the conventional multihead architecture.
Based on these objectives, the main contributions of this work are:
• 
Hierarchical multitask architecture for event–scene modeling: We introduce a hierarchical alternative to the conventional multihead architecture for joint ASC-AT learning, in which the intermediate event representation is explicitly used to condition the scene prediction. This architecture provides a direct pathway for analyzing the relationship between acoustic events and scenes.
• 
Comprehensive large-scale benchmark: Rather than introducing isolated models, we conduct an extensive empirical benchmark comprising 66 full training runs across three state-of-the-art pretrained backbones (PaSST, PANNs, and BEATs) under exhaustive loss-weighting regimes (β∈[0.0,1.0]\beta\in[0.0,1.0]), providing the first systematic study of architectural topology in joint ASC-AT tasks.
• 
Synchronous multitask learning dynamics: We find a fundamental difference in optimization behavior on this dataset: while multihead models sequentially master the easier ASC task before optimizing AT, the hierarchical paradigm achieves synchronized dual-task learning across balanced loss weights (β∈[0.6,0.9]\beta\in[0.6,0.9]), leading to more stable joint representations.
• 
Multi-perspective analysis of event-scene representations: We introduce a multi-perspective interpretability framework combining information bottleneck metrics (H⁡(E|S)H(E|S), I⁡(E,S)I(E;S)), manifold geometry (Silhouette Score over P⁡(E|S)P(E|S)), and FCA on TF-IDF weighted event matrices to evaluate how discrete acoustic concepts are preserved through the intermediate bottleneck.
II Related Work
ASC, SED, and AT have been extensively studied within the DCASE community [3]. In recent years, ASC research has increasingly focused not only on classification performance but also on computational efficiency. In the 2023 DCASE challenge, Schmid et al. [15] proposed a knowledge-distillation approach that achieved the best performance in the challenge, using PaSST [16] as teacher model. PaSST is an efficient and high-capacity transformer architecture that has subsequently become widely adopted for acoustic scene analysis [17]. In SED and AT, large-scale pretrained audio encoders such as PANNs [18], trained on AudioSet [19], have become standard architectures for learning general-purpose acoustic representations. Their representations have also been incorporated into more complex multimodal and audio-language systems, such as Large-Scale Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining with Feature Fusion and Keyword-to-Caption Augmentation (CLAP) [20].
Regarding databases, one of the most well-known in this field is AudioSet [19], which contains human-labeled 10-second sound clips extracted from 2, 084, 320 YouTube videos. There are also other databases widely used for AT and SED, such as FSD50K [21] or DESED [22]; this last one is specialized in domestic sounds and has been used since DCASE 2020. Similarly, in 2024, WildDESED [23] was created; an extension of the original DESED dataset to reflect a wider variety of domestic scenarios by incorporating complex and unpredictable background noises.
On the other hand, the TAU Urban Acoustic Scenes 2022 Mobile Development Data Set [24] was selected for the ASC task since 2022. Similarly, other ASC datasets such as TUT Urban Acoustic Scenes 2018 [7] have been used for years in the DCASE challenge.
Despite the close complementarity between ASC, SED, and AT, these tasks have traditionally been investigated independently, overlooking the potentially informative relationships between acoustic events and the environments in which they occur. This has motivated the application of multitask learning to jointly exploit scene- and event-level information. Tonami et al. [12] investigated joint ASC and event recognition as a multitask problem, providing an early baseline for learning both types of information from shared acoustic representations. To this end, they adapted the TUT Sound Events 2016/2017 and TUT Acoustic Scenes 2016 [25], [8] datasets to this joint learning setting.
Subsequent studies also adopted this baseline and explored different mechanisms for exploiting the interaction between the tasks. Imoto et al. [13] introduced soft scene labels generated by a teacher model to improve joint learning, while Igarashi et al. [14] investigated semi-supervised joint learning by incorporating weak event labels. Other approaches have explored additional sources of information, such as semantic scene context [26], adversarial training [27], balanced multitask objectives [28], and scene-dependent representations [29]. More broadly, joint learning of ASC, SED, and AT has also been investigated within the DCASE community, demonstrating the potential of multitask representations to capture complementary information across acoustic tasks.
A particularly relevant line of research explicitly models the relationship between acoustic events and scenes. Hou et al. [30] proposed Relation-Guided Acoustic Scene Classification (RGASC), in which event embeddings obtained from PANNs are used to construct an event–scene relation matrix that guides scene classification. This idea was further developed by Hou et al. [31] using additional pretraining on the JSSED synthetic dataset. These approaches demonstrate that event-level information can provide useful contextual cues for ASC beyond conventional shared representations. However, their primary objective is to use event information to improve scene classification, rather than to characterize how the learned representation itself encodes the underlying event–scene relationships.
There is a great deal of research focused on training neural networks through an analysis based on information theory. One of the best-known researchers in this field is Naftali Tishby, who proposed the Information Bottleneck in 2000 [11]. This is a theoretical principle in machine learning and information theory, and the main idea is that learning can be understood as a process of compressing information. The goal is to find a representation of the XX data that retains only the information relevant to predicting a target variable YY, while discarding irrelevant information.
In 2019, Tishby explained his groundbreaking proposal at the Conference on the Mathematical Theory of Deep Learning (DeepMath 2019), where he described the two phases of neural network training [32]. Letting TT be a latent variable, he identified a first fitting phase in which the network memorizes the input information, increasing both I⁡(X,T)I(X;T) and I⁡(T,Y)I(T;Y) simultaneously. Afterwards, there is a second compression phase where the network discards irrelevant information and generalizes, reducing I⁡(X,T)I(X;T) while I⁡(T,Y)I(T;Y) remains at a similar level.
Moreover, deeper architectures tend to reach the compression regime faster, as multiple layers facilitate hierarchical abstraction [33].
Following the analysis of relationships between acoustic events and scenes, FCA provides a natural formal framework for representing object–attribute relations through concept lattices, making their underlying structure explicit [34, 35].
Additionally, beyond joint deep representations, techniques from Information Retrieval (IR) offer an explicit framework for measuring the occurrence and relevance of discrete acoustic elements within larger acoustic environments. In particular, the TF-IDF [36] formulation—traditionally used in text processing—has been adapted to audio analysis by modeling acoustic scenes as ”documents” and detected sound events or acoustic words as ”terms” [37, 38]. Frameworks based on Bag-of-Audio-Words (BoAW) [39] and event-based semantic vectors use TF-IDF to reduce the importance of common, uninformative background sounds while emphasizing distinctive events that strongly characterize a specific scene [38]. In a sequential audio retrieval and classification paradigm—where sound events are predicted before scene inference—TF-IDF provides an interpretable intermediate layer. It quantifies how informative the predicted event sequence is about the underlying scene, establishing an explicit information-theoretic bridge to evaluate how effectively discrete event representations transmit the necessary context for downstream scene analysis.
Despite the continuous progress in multitask audio representation learning, no prior work has proposed a strictly hierarchical, sequential framework that analyzes the bottleneck of acoustic event representations through the combined approaches of Information Theory and Information Retrieval. Most existing literature focuses primarily on proposing novel multi-head or joint-learning architectures aimed at maximizing classification metrics. Consequently, fundamental research on how acoustic events and scenes interact within a single representation is lacking, particularly on datasets of this nature. While Hou et al. [30] introduced RGASC to model event-scene dependencies via a relation matrix constructed from PANN embeddings, their approach uses event information only as a contextual feature, not as a strict sequential bottleneck.
In this work, we address this gap by introducing a hierarchical multitask architecture in which the intermediate event representation explicitly conditions the scene prediction, and by systematically comparing it with the conventional multihead architecture across multiple pretrained audio backbones and loss-weighting configurations. Beyond predictive performance, we analyze the resulting representations from complementary information-theoretic, geometric, and semantic perspectives, combining entropy and mutual information measures, representation geometry, and TF-IDF-based FCA to examine how event-scene relationships are preserved through the learned bottleneck.

III-B Event-Scene Relationship Analysis via FCA Lattices
To better understand the relationship between sound events and acoustic scenes, we employ FCA as a complementary analysis of the dataset. FCA provides a mathematical framework to identify groups of attributes that tend to occur together across a set of objects. In our case, each acoustic scene is considered an object, while the sound-event labels are treated as attributes. A binary formal context is constructed by indicating whether a given sound event accounts for a sufficient proportion of the scene duration. This representation allows us to identify recurring combinations of sound events and to characterize the acoustic composition of the different scenes.
For each acoustic scene, we compute a sound presence matrix describing the relative temporal prevalence of each sound event. The total duration associated with each event is obtained by summing its annotated durations across all audio recordings belonging to a given scene. These values are then normalized by the total duration of the corresponding scene, resulting in a scene–event matrix whose entries represent the proportion of the scene duration associated with each event. This matrix is used to construct the binary formal contexts by applying a threshold φ\varphi; after inspecting the resulting prior distributions, we set φ=0.15\varphi=0.15 to obtain the formal contexts used for the FCA analysis. Fig. 4 shows the sound presence matrix, the lattice applied to it, and the lattice applied to the TF-IDF transformation of the prior matrix, for the development and evaluation sets.
To obtain a more discriminative view, we additionally apply a TF-IDF transformation to the scene–event matrix, treating each scene as a document and each event as a term whose frequency is given by its relative temporal prevalence. The inverse document frequency factor down-weights events that occur across many scenes (e.g., ”people walking”, present in three of the four scenes), while the subsequent per-scene L2 normalization expresses each weight relative to the overall event profile of that scene. Consequently, an event only exceeds φ\varphi when it is both prevalent within a scene and specific to it, so the same threshold selects discriminative event–scene associations rather than merely frequent ones. Note that, because of this normalization, TF-IDF can also promote weak but specific events in scenes with sparse event profiles, and demote secondary events in scenes with many dominant events.

In Fig. 4, we see that this dataset contains many events that are highly representative of a particular acoustic scene. For example, both ”breathing” and ”fan” appear exclusively in the ”office” scene in the development set. More generally, the raw lattices (Fig. 4 (b,e)) show that each scene is characterized by a block of exclusive events attached directly to its object concept: domestic activity sounds (”water tap running”, ”washing dishes”, ”glass jingling”, ”drawer”, ”dishes”, ”cutlery”, ”cupboard”, ”snapping”) for ”home”; computer-related sounds (”keyboard typing”, ”mouse clicking”, ”mouse wheeling”) together with ”fan” and ”breathing” for ”office”; traffic sounds (”large vehicle”, ”brakes squeaking”) for ”city center”; and natural or outdoor sounds (”wind blowing”, ”bird singing”, ”banging”) for ”residential area”.
Above these scene-specific concepts, the lattices reveal a small number of shared concepts that capture the overlap between scenes. The events ”impact” and ”rustling” group ”home” and ”office” into an indoor concept related to object manipulation, whereas ”car” (and ”children” in the development set) groups ”city center” and ”residential area” into an outdoor concept. ”People walking” is the most widespread event, linking ”home” with both outdoor scenes, while ”people talking” links ”office” with the outdoor scenes. The latter creates crossing relationships between the indoor and outdoor branches, so the raw lattices (10 concepts each) do not follow a clean hierarchical structure. The outdoor scenes share the largest number of events (e.g., four of the six events of ”city center” in the development set are also present in ”residential area”), which suggests that this pair is the most acoustically confusable.
The TF-IDF lattices (Fig. 4 (c,f)) simplify this structure to 9 concepts. Since ”people talking” is no longer associated with ”office”, the indoor and outdoor branches become clearly separated: ”home” and ”office” are joined only by ”impact”, ”city center” and ”residential area” by ”car” (together with ”people talking” in the development set and ”bird singing” in the evaluation set), and ”people walking” remains the only bridge between ”home” and the outdoor scenes. In addition, events that were shared by two scenes are assigned to the scene where they are more prevalent. For instance, ”children” becomes exclusive to ”city center” in the development set, and ”rustling” becomes exclusive to ”home” in the development set but to ”office” in the evaluation set. This last case illustrates that some events are genuinely ambiguous between scenes, and that their discriminative value depends on the subset considered.
Comparing both subsets, the core structure is stable: the exclusive event blocks of each scene, the outdoor concept defined by ”car”, the indoor concept defined by ”impact”, and the bridging role of ”people walking” appear in all four lattices. The differences are concentrated in low-prevalence events whose values lie close to φ\varphi, such as ”children”, ”squeaking”, and ”breathing”. ”Squeaking”, for example, is not associated with any scene in the development set but appears in ”office” in the raw evaluation lattice, while ”breathing” and ”squeaking” fall below the threshold after the TF-IDF transformation in the evaluation set. Conversely, ”bird singing” reaches ”city center” in the evaluation set only after TF-IDF, owing to the sparse event profile of this scene. Overall, the lattices show that acoustic scenes are largely defined by specific combinations of sound events organized around a few shared concepts, which supports conditioning scene predictions on intermediate event probabilities, as in the proposed hierarchical architecture.

IV-A2 BEATs
Similar to PaSST, BEATs (Bidirectional Encoder representation from Audio Transformers) employs a ViT architecture as its backbone, using a linear projection layer followed by a stack of Transformer encoder layers to process sequences of audio patches. In contrast to conventional audio pre-training approaches based on acoustic feature reconstruction, BEATs is pre-trained through a Masked Audio Modeling (MAM) objective, where masked audio patches are used to predict discrete acoustic tokens generated by an iterative acoustic tokenizer. The acoustic tokenizer and the audio SSL model are iteratively optimized through knowledge distillation, allowing both components to improve their representations progressively. They then fine-tune the resulting audio representation model for downstream audio classification tasks by replacing the pre-training label predictor with a task-specific linear classifier [41]. In this work, we use the BEATs model pre-trained on AudioSet as a checkpoint and replace its final linear classification layer with two alternative architectures: a hierarchical sequential architecture and a multi-head architecture, following the same strategy used for the other backbone models.
IV-A3 PANNs
These models constitute one of the most widely used families of neural networks for general-purpose audio classification and sound event recognition. Although introduced before the growth of attention and Transformer-based architectures, PANNs models remain highly competitive and continue to be widely adopted as audio encoders in more complex multimodal and audio-language systems, such as CLAP [20]. Their strong performance, robustness across different audio domains, and availability of pre-trained models make PANNs a relevant convolutional baseline for comparison with more recent Transformer-based architectures. In this work, we use a pre-trained PANNs model as one of the backbone architectures and adapt its final classification layer to the two proposed configurations: the hierarchical sequential architecture and the multi-head architecture.

IV-C Information-Theoretic Framework
According to Naftali Tishby’s theory about the information bottleneck [11], learning can be understood as a process of compressing information. Given that XX represents the input data, the goal is to find a latent variable TT that retains only the information relevant to predict a target variable YY. In 20192019, Thisby proposed the two phases of neural network training at the Conference on the Mathematical Theory of Deep Learning (DeepMath 2019) [32]. He identified a first fitting phase in which the network memorizes the input information, increasing both I⁡(X,T)I(X;T) and I⁡(T,Y)I(T;Y) simultaneously. Afterwards, there is a second compression phase where the network discards irrelevant information and generalizes, reducing I⁡(X,T)I(X;T) while I⁡(T,Y)I(T;Y) remains at a similar level.
In our multitask formulation, we adapt this framework by forcing the intermediate latent representation TT to explicitly represent the predicted acoustic event space EE, while the target variable YY corresponds to the acoustic scene SS. The input audio signal XX is processed by the deep backbone until it is compressed into this intermediate event-level probability space EE. This event space acts as the functional information bottleneck of our system: the network must discard noisy acoustic variability from XX while retaining only the sound event descriptors necessary to predict the scene SS.
Under this formal mapping, the event-related loss ℒevent\mathcal{L}_{\text{event}} governs the mutual information I⁡(X,E)I(X;E) between the raw acoustic features and the learned event concepts, whereas the scene-related loss ℒscene\mathcal{L}_{\text{scene}} optimizes the information I⁡(E,S)I(E;S) transmitted from the event bottleneck to the final scene predictions. Fundamentally, in our proposed hierarchical topology, the scene classification layer receives the predicted event probability distribution EE as its input, without direct access to the raw acoustic features XX. This architecture physically forces the information flow through the sequence X→E→SX\to E\to S, as illustrated in Fig. 8.
For evaluation purposes, while the hierarchical architecture establishes an explicit physical bottleneck, the unconstrained multihead baseline outputs event EE and scene SS predictions via parallel heads branching from a shared feature representation. To enable a fair comparison, we extract the event probability matrix synthesized by the multihead model and construct its conditional event distribution P⁡(E∣S)P(E\mid S) post-hoc. This allows us to examine the implicit information bottleneck formed by the multihead joint space, evaluating whether its learned event representations naturally compress and structure scene-relevant information under the same information-theoretic metrics.

In terms of overall performance, there are no significant differences between the multihead and hierarchical architectures in the ASC task; PaSST achieves better results using the hierarchical architecture, while BEATs do the contrary, and PANNs maintains similar metrics. VI-B Training Dynamics across Loss Weighting (β\beta)
Fig. 9 shows the evaluation performance over training epochs in terms of accuracy for ASC and macro F1-score for AT. Each trajectory represents a specific β\beta value, illustrating how the weighting factor influences training dynamics.
These trajectories reveal interesting patterns from an information-compression perspective. For the multihead architecture, the model initially prioritizes the simpler task, ASC. Once a baseline representation for ASC is established, it begins learning the more complex task, AT. Visually, this sequential optimization causes the performance paths to shift rightward first along the ASC axis before moving upward along the AT axis.
A key finding of this study is that this decoupled learning behavior does not occur in the hierarchical architecture, particularly for higher β\beta values (0.6≤β≤0.90.6\leq\beta\leq 0.9) that favor the AT task. In these cases, performance on both tasks increases simultaneously, indicating that learning AT features directly drives and optimizes the underlying representation needed for ASC.
This joint convergence suggests that the hierarchical bottleneck forces the model to compress event-level details into a shared representation that immediately benefits scene inference, rather than learning two isolated tasks as observed in the multihead setup.
Additionally, Fig. 9 further supports our previous observation regarding the lack of a clear performance gap between multihead and hierarchical architectures. The endpoints of the trajectories—representing peak performance across both metrics—reach very similar regions in the task-space. Minor advantages in either ASC accuracy or AT F1-score are heavily dependent on early stopping criteria or specific hyperparameter setups rather than an intrinsic architectural superiority.

VI-C Information Bottleneck and Representation Profiling
To evaluate how intermediate event representations organize and transmit scene-discriminative information, Fig. 10 illustrates the mean conditional entropy H¯​(E∣S)\bar{H}(E\mid S), mutual information I⁡(E,S)I(E;S), and Kullback–Leibler divergence DKL(PH∥PM)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\mathrm{H}}\parallel P_{\mathrm{M}}) across all three model backbones (PaSST, PANNs, and BEATs) as a function of the multitask loss weight β\beta.
Across almost all models and hyperparameter configurations (β\beta), the proposed hierarchical architecture consistently yields a lower conditional mean entropy H¯​(E∣S)\bar{H}(E\mid S) compared to the multihead baseline. In accordance with the information bottleneck principle, this lower entropy indicates that hierarchical conditioning effectively acts as a structural regularizer, suppressing diffuse background event activations and focusing the probability mass onto a compact, scene-specific subset of acoustic triggers.
Additionally, this spatial compression does not degrade semantic fidelity. As shown in Fig. 10, the hierarchical architecture achieves systematically higher mutual information I⁡(E,S)I(E;S) across most β\beta values. This confirms that while the hierarchical mechanism prunes irrelevant event noise, it preserves the statistical dependence between the intermediate event predictions and the target scene categories. Consequently, the intermediate event layer serves as a highly discriminative acoustic bottleneck.
Finally, the Kullback-Leibler divergence DKL(PH∥PM)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\mathrm{H}}\parallel P_{\mathrm{M}}) evaluates the structural distance between the final converged event distributions of both architectures. Across all models, DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} reaches a minimum at β=0.9\beta=0.9. While the training trajectories of the hierarchical and multihead models differ significantly throughout optimization (shown in Fig. 9), their final converged representations become remarkably similar under this configuration. At β=0.9\beta=0.9, event loss dominates the total loss. This forces both architectures to prioritize fitting raw event labels, minimizing the structural effect of the hierarchical head and yielding almost identical final event distributions. However, for β<0.9\beta<0.9, the hierarchical constraint successfully shapes the representation space, keeping it structurally distinct from the multihead baseline.

VI-E Semantic Concept Preservation via Formal Concept Analysis
While information-theoretic and geometric metrics summarize global representation quality, they do not explicitly reveal which semantic associations are learned or corrupted by the model. To bridge this interpretability gap, we construct FCA concept lattices from the TF-IDF-weighted event predictions and compare them directly against the ground-truth context lattice (Fig. 4 (f)). By minimizing background noise via TF-IDF, FCA isolates the structural hierarchy of highly discriminative acoustic concepts.
Fig. 12 shows the lattices obtained from the predictions of the six models on the evaluation set, which can be compared with the ground-truth TF-IDF lattice in Fig. 12 (f). All predicted lattices are sparser than the ground truth: they contain 8 or 9 concepts and recover between 11 and 22 of the 28 event–scene incidences of the reference context, while introducing very few spurious associations (at most three per model). This indicates that the models behave conservatively, retaining only the associations for which they provide the strongest and most specific evidence. Nevertheless, the backbone of the ground-truth structure is preserved in all cases: ”car” remains the concept shared by ”city center” and ”residential area”, ”impact” remains the concept shared by ”home” and ”office”, and each scene keeps a set of characteristic exclusive events, such as ”large vehicle” for ”city center”, ”bird singing” for ”residential area”, ”water tap running” and ”washing dishes” for ”home”, and ”fan”, ”keyboard typing”, and ”mouse clicking” for ”office”.
Fig. 12: FCA lattices constructed from the TF-IDF-weighted event-scene relationship matrices predicted by the models, using a threshold of φ=0.15\varphi=0.15. The top row (a-c) corresponds to the hierarchical architecture, while the bottom row (d-f) corresponds to the multihead architecture. From left to right, columns correspond to PANNs, PaSST, and BEATs, respectively.
The main structural difference between both architectures concerns ”people walking”, the most widespread and therefore least discriminative event in the ground truth, where it links ”home” with both outdoor scenes. In the hierarchical models, this event is never shared across scenes: it is either assigned exclusively to ”city center” (PANNs and BEATs) or discarded (PaSST). In contrast, two of the three multihead models retain it as a shared attribute, either between the two outdoor scenes (PANNs) or across ”home”, ”city center”, and ”residential area” (BEATs), thus reproducing the crossing link between the indoor and outdoor branches. As a result, the hierarchical lattices of PaSST and BEATs reduce to two clearly separated branches, indoor and outdoor, that only meet at the top concept. This behavior is consistent with the lower conditional entropy H⁡(E|S)H(E|S) observed for the hierarchical models: by concentrating the predicted event distribution of each scene on fewer and more specific events, hierarchical conditioning suppresses frequent associations but carries little information about the scene.
The amount of detail retained, however, depends on the backbone. The hierarchical PaSST model yields the most compact lattice, recovering only 11 incidences, whereas the hierarchical PANNs model yields the richest one, with 22 correct incidences and the highest agreement with the ground truth among all models. It is also the only model that recovers ”children” and ”banging” in ”residential area” and ”rustling” in ”office”, the latter being one of the ambiguous events identified in Section III-B. In exchange, it introduces a spurious association between ”dishes” and ”city center”, which creates a link between ”home” and ”city center” absent from the ground truth. It also assigns ”people talking” to ”city center” and ”breathing” to ”office”, associations that appear in the development set (Fig. 4 (c)) but not in the evaluation set. Consequently, at the level of individual incidences, neither architecture is uniformly superior: the hierarchical models achieve higher agreement for PANNs and BEATs, while the multihead model does so for PaSST.
Finally, some ground-truth associations are missed by all models, notably ”glass jingling” in ”home”, ”mouse wheeling” in ”office”, and ”people talking” in ”residential area”. ”Residential area” is the scene with the largest loss, retaining at most four of its seven associated events. These correspond mostly to low-prevalence or acoustically ambiguous events, whose predicted probabilities rarely exceed φ\varphi after TF-IDF weighting. Likewise, no model associates ”bird singing” with ”city center”, an association that in the ground truth arises only from the normalization of a weak event (Section III-B). Overall, these results support that hierarchical conditioning preserves the key event–scene relationships of the ground truth while discarding less informative shared associations, although the level of detail retained strongly depends on the backbone.
VII Limitations and Future Work
While our systematic benchmark provides critical insights into the optimization dynamics and latent geometry of multitask acoustic models, several limitations remain to be addressed in subsequent research:
1. 
Dataset Lack and Domain Generalization. High-quality datasets offering simultaneous, aligned annotations for both broad acoustic scenes and fine-grained audio events are exceptionally lacking in the audio community. Consequently, our findings are based on a single benchmark dataset. Evaluating whether these representation properties hold in larger-scale, highly unconstrained, or open-set acoustic environments remains an important next step.
2. 
Potential Loss of Acoustic Gist. By routing scene classification exclusively through the intermediate event probability matrix P⁡(E∣S)P(E\mid S), the hierarchical architecture enforces a strict information bottleneck. If the pre-defined event vocabulary fails to capture fine background textures—the global acoustic gist of an environment—there is a risk of error propagation from missed event triggers to final scene predictions.
3. 
Computational Overhead of Hyperparameter Sweeping. Exhaustively exploring the joint trade-off space across multiple backbone architectures required significant compute resources (66 full training runs). Developing dynamic loss-weighting algorithms that automatically balance task learning without requiring offline grid searches represents a key optimization challenge.
To build upon these findings, future work will focus on three main directions. First, we plan to extend this interpretability framework by analyzing the relationship between ASC and SED, instead of AT. Second, we aim to investigate hybrid architectures that combine the structured intermediate event bottleneck P⁡(E∣S)P(E\mid S) with a residual global feature bypass to preserve ambient acoustic context. Finally, we will explore self-supervised pre-training strategies to expand the intermediate event vocabulary, reducing the risk of domain-specific information bottlenecks.
VIII Conclusion
In this paper, we addressed the limitations of standard unconstrained multihead architectures for joint ASC and AT by proposing a hierarchical (sequential) conditioning framework. By conditioning scene predictions directly on intermediate, normalized event probability distributions P⁡(E∣S)P(E\mid S), our approach aligns model structure with the intrinsic hierarchy of physical acoustic environments.
Through an extensive empirical evaluation encompassing 66 full training runs across three state-of-the-art backbones (PaSST, PANNs, and BEATs), we demonstrated that hierarchical conditioning achieves competitive overall classification metrics while fundamentally stabilizing multitask optimization. Crucially, optimization dynamics reveal that whereas multihead architectures master the simpler ASC task early before optimizing AT, the Hierarchical approach fosters synchronized dual-task learning across balanced loss weights (β∈[0.6,0.9]\beta\in[0.6,0.9]).
Furthermore, our multi-perspective interpretability framework—combining information-theoretic bottleneck metrics, manifold geometry analysis, and FCA on TF-IDF event activations—shows that the hierarchical paradigm produces a more structured intermediate representation space. Across model architectures, hierarchical conditioning consistently yields lower conditional entropy H⁡(E∣S)H(E\mid S), higher mutual information I⁡(E,S)I(E;S), and tighter latent cluster separability (higher Silhouette scores). The FCA lattices further show that hierarchical models preserve key event-scene relationships from the ground truth while reducing less informative associations, providing an interpretable view of the semantic structure learned by the models.

Abstract
Objective:
Absolute auditory attention decoding (aAAD) aims to track how strongly a listener attends to a single speech source using electroencephalography (EEG). Unlike selective auditory attention decoding, aAAD lacks a competing speech reference, making reliable attention tracking challenging.
Approach:
We propose a fully unsupervised aAAD pipeline combining neural envelope tracking (NET) with hidden Markov model (HMM)-based temporal inference. Using EEG signals and the target speech envelope, the framework estimates a continuous attention trajectory without explicit attention-state labels. We evaluate the approach using EEG recordings from 30 adults, investigate the impact of analysis window length, and compare HMM post-processing with moving-average (MA) smoothing and alternative EEG features.
Main results:
With 1-s analysis windows, non-causal HMM post-processing improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for all 30 participants, increasing mean AUC from 0.547 for raw NET to 0.832. A 5-s window achieves the highest mean AUC of 0.858. Compared with non-causal MA smoothing, the HMM achieves higher AUC across the examined smoothing scales. Individual switch detection times are comparable, while the HMM generally achieves lower group-level detection times. NET also outperforms alpha power and spectral entropy as an observation feature in the unsupervised HMM framework.
Significance:
The proposed framework provides a label-free approach for estimating temporal fluctuations in auditory attention, demonstrating the utility of probabilistic temporal inference for continuous attention tracking in single-speaker listening scenarios.
Index Terms: Absolute auditory attention decoding, neural envelope tracking, hidden Markov model, unsupervised temporal inference, EEG.
I Introduction
Auditory attention plays a crucial role in contexts such as classroom environments, where the instructor’s voice often acts as the primary attractor. However, attention is not a static cognitive state; instead, it fluctuates over time and is influenced by factors such as distractions, fatigue [1], and mind wandering [2]. Understanding how auditory attention evolves over time can therefore provide valuable insights into learning processes in the classroom and enable applications such as attention monitoring systems that track students’ engagement dynamics and provide student-specific feedback [3].
In the past decade, extensive research has demonstrated that auditory attention to natural speech can be decoded from EEG signals with stimulus reconstruction approaches [4, 5, 6, 7].
Compared to commonly used EEG markers associated with attention such as alpha power [8, 9] and spectral entropy [10], neural envelope tracking (NET) has been regarded as a stimulus-specific metric of auditory attention, as it reflects neural responses to the speech signal itself rather than general mental effort [11, 10, 12]. To compute the NET metric, a neural decoder is trained to reconstruct the temporal envelope of the attended speech from EEG recordings, and the Pearson correlation between the reconstructed envelope and the corresponding speech envelope is used as a measure of auditory attention. This NET-based approach has been successfully applied in selective auditory attention decoding (sAAD) [4, 6, 5] and absolute auditory attention decoding (aAAD) paradigms [11, 13, 14, 15].
In sAAD, attention is measured by comparing correlations across multiple competing speakers, with the speaker yielding the highest correlation identified as the attended one. In contrast, aAAD considers scenarios in which only a single speech stream is present and aims to continuously track how attention to this target evolves over time. It directly uses the NET score as a measure of the degree of attention to the target speaker. However, as there is no relative reference from competing speakers to compare with, aAAD poses a fundamentally more challenging inference problem than sAAD, as attention must be estimated from a single, neural evidence stream.
Moreover, instantaneous NET estimates are typically noisy, in particular when measured over short time intervals. They can also be influenced by confounding factors that are not attention-driven, such as temporal variations in the dynamic range of the speech envelope [13, 16]. As a result, raw NET values can be difficult to interpret directly on a window-by-window basis.
Motivated by these limitations, it is therefore natural to post-process the NET score by treating the NET sequence as a time series and applying smoothing techniques that take temporal coherence into account. This is reasonable because attention states in neighboring windows are not expected to be independent, especially when the window length is short. Instead, attention is likely to be piecewise stable in natural learning scenarios, as people are unlikely to switch attention every second and tend to remain focused on the target for at least several seconds, or even minutes [17].
In this work, we present a modular aAAD pipeline that combines NET-based evidence extraction with probabilistic temporal inference based on a hidden Markov model (HMM), a powerful framework that is able to infer attention states from NET observations, inspired by similar work in sAAD [18]. The proposed pipeline is designed for off-line analysis and is fully unsupervised (i.e., no attention labels are used for training), relying only on a small set of tunable and interpretable parameters.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the proposed aAAD pipeline, including the NET-based evidence extraction module and the HMM-based temporal inference module. Section III describes the experimental protocol, EEG preprocessing procedure, evaluation metrics, and default parameter settings. Section IV presents the experimental validation of the proposed framework. We first demonstrate the added value of HMM post-processing compared with raw NET, and then analyze the effect of analysis window length on the area under the curve (AUC) and switch detection time (SDT). We further compare the HMM with moving-average (MA) smoothing to assess the advantage of state-based temporal inference over fixed-window averaging. Finally, we compare NET with alpha power and spectral entropy as observation features for the unsupervised HMM framework. Section V concludes the paper.
II Methodology
II-A Pipeline Overview
This section presents an overview of the proposed pipeline for off-line analysis of absolute auditory attention, which is conceptually visualized in Fig. 1. The pipeline operates in a fully unsupervised manner and is controlled by a small set of interpretable parameters.
Starting from the input EEG recordings and the target speech signal, the proposed pipeline first performs EEG pre-processing and speech envelope extraction, followed by neural decoding to compute a windowed neural envelope tracking (NET) sequence, which serves as stimulus-specific evidence of attention to the target speech. Concretely, a linear spatio-temporal decoder is first trained to extract the neural responses to the target speech, thereby removing irrelevant EEG signal components. To this end, we use the so-called stimulus-reconstruction paradigm, which aims to reconstruct the speech envelope from the pre-processed EEG by solving a least-squares regression problem on all data. The trained decoder is then applied to the EEG to obtain a reconstructed envelope, which is compared with the target speech envelope using the Pearson correlation coefficient computed over multiple non-overlapping11
 1
 We use non-overlapping windows, as the HMM post-processing assumes independent observations. windows. The resulting correlation values form the NET sequence. Although a linear least-squares decoder is used in this work, the proposed pipeline is not restricted to a specific decoding method, and any alternative linear or nonlinear decoder (e.g., CCA-based [19] or neural network-based models [20, 21]) can be incorporated, as long as it provides a correlation-based neural tracking metric between EEG and the target stimulus. Next, an HMM is applied to the NET sequence—using either causal or non-causal inference—to explicitly model temporal dependencies and obtain a smoothed attention estimate in the form of the posterior probability of being attentive. This posterior probability is finally reported as the continuous attention score over time. Importantly, both the neural evidence extraction and the temporal inference stages operate without requiring attention-state labels.
Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed aAAD pipeline.
II-B Evidence Extraction Module: Neural Envelope Tracking
II-B1 Neural Decoder Design
Similar to [4, 6, 5, 11, 13], we adopt a spatio-temporal linear decoder that aims to reconstruct the speech envelope of the presented stimulus from the EEG of the participant. In this work, the speech envelope is extracted using the power law and gammatone filterbank procedure proposed in [22], yet any envelope extraction method can be used.
