After training, the decoder is applied to the same segments of the same participant, which are segmented into windows indexed by tt. For each window tt, the EEG data is represented as 𝐗(t)∈ℝN×L​C\mathbf{X}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times LC}, where NN denotes the number of time samples within that analysis window. We define the Pearson correlation coefficient between the reconstructed and true speech envelope ρ⁡(𝐬^(t),𝐬(t))\rho\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t)}\right) as the neural envelope tracking (NET) metric for window tt [11]. It was demonstrated in [11, 12, 13, 14] that higher NET values on average correspond to a higher level of attention to the target speech.
II-B2 Label-Free Decoder Training
In this work, the neural decoder is trained using all available data and subsequently applied to the same dataset to compute the Pearson correlation between the reconstructed and the true speech envelope on a window-by-window basis. This validation strategy differs from many previous studies [22, 20, 18, 23], where a strict train-test split is enforced. Nevertheless, we argue that it is appropriate for the present aAAD setting, as previous work has demonstrated the feasibility of unsupervised aAAD without a separate training dataset [24].
Specifically, the decoder is designed to capture the stimulus-response relationship between EEG signals and the speech envelope, rather than to explicitly discriminate between attentive and inattentive states. Under this formulation, inattentive EEG does not correspond to a distinct neural pattern, but rather to a weaker or noisier manifestation of the same stimulus-driven neural response. Accordingly, we adopt the perspective that aAAD is better formulated as a signal matching problem with attention-dependent signal-to-noise ratios, rather than as a binary classification problem with separable EEG patterns.
Within this framework, correlation-based evaluation provides a meaningful measure of neural tracking strength, even when the decoder is applied to the same data used for training. This formulation constitutes one of the key ingredients that enables a fully unsupervised aAAD framework, as it allows stimulus-specific neural evidence to be extracted without requiring explicit attention labels.
It should be noted that the training of the neural decoder requires sufficient baseline data during which the participant actually attends to the speech, in order to reliably estimate the stimulus–response mapping. If the available baseline segments are too limited in duration, the estimated decoder may become unstable, which can subsequently affect the quality of the neural tracking feature used for temporal inference.
II-C Temporal Inference Module
Given a NET sequence (containing one NET value for each window tt), we employ a hidden Markov model (HMM) as a temporal inference
module to obtain a smooth estimate of the underlying attention dynamics, inspired by similar work in sAAD [18].
The HMM takes the NET sequence as its sole observation input and infers a latent attention
state sequence that evolves over time. We note that the temporal inference module
operates independently of how the NET sequence is obtained. Although NET is computed in this work
using a linear neural decoding model, the HMM can in principle be applied to any stimulus-specific
evidence sequence derived from linear or non-linear models [18].
II-C1 Markov Chain Background

Building on the Markov chain model above, we formulate an HMM by introducing a probabilistic

This modeling choice reflects two key characteristics of attentional dynamics: (1) attentional engagement exhibits temporal persistence rather than arbitrary rapid transitions, and (2) the distribution of NET observations is state-dependent. Emission Model
To perform HMM inference, we specify the emission (observation) model
p⁡(y⁡(t)∣S⁡(t))p(y(t)\mid S(t)), where y⁡(t)y(t) denotes the scalar NET-based observation at time tt.
Specifically, the NET observation is obtained from the correlation-based metric after
applying the Fisher transformation
y⁡(t)=atanh⁡(r⁡(t)),y(t)=\mathrm{atanh}\big(r(t)\big),
(22)
where r⁡(t)r(t) denotes the raw Pearson correlation coefficient. After the Fisher
transformation, correlation coefficients are approximately normally distributed [25, 26],
which motivates the use of Gaussian emission models.
Accordingly, we model the emission probability bi​(t)b_{i}(t) required by the inference algorithm as:
p⁡(y⁡(t)∣S⁡(t)=Si)=𝒩⁡(y⁡(t),μi,σ2),p\big(y(t)\mid S(t)=S_{i}\big)=\mathcal{N}\!\big(y(t);\mu_{i},\sigma^{2}\big),
(23)
where μi\mu_{i} is the state-dependent mean and σ2\sigma^{2} is a variance shared across both states.
The tied-variance assumption reduces the number of free parameters and improves numerical
robustness, and was shown to be realistic in sAAD [27].
Under the Gaussian emission assumption in (23), the emission parameters
can be estimated directly from the observed sequence in an unsupervised manner. Specifically, for
each participant, we use a multiscale two-component Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with shared variance
to estimate the emission parameters from observations computed at multiple window lengths
(55, 1010, and 3030 s), following the multiscale fitting strategy in [28].
The key idea is to estimate common state-dependent means while accounting for the fact that the
variance of Fisher-transformed correlation estimates decreases with increasing window length.
Accordingly, the GMM estimates shared component means and a common variance scale, which is then
converted to the emission variance corresponding to the analysis window length used for HMM inference.
The GMM parameters are estimated using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm
[29]. The resulting component means and window-length-adjusted variance are
then used to define the HMM emission parameters (μ1,μ2,σ2)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\sigma^{2}).
III Experiment and Evaluation
III-A Protocol Design
The experimental protocol is described in detail in [14]. Briefly, EEG was recorded while 30 participants watched a 75-minute video lecture on “neuromyths”, common but false beliefs about the brain. The video only shows the teacher in front of PowerPoint slides (mainly images with hardly any text) and the content was explained entirely through speech. The video was divided into eight parts of 10 minutes each (except the first part, which is only 5 minutes), separated by short breaks (see Fig. 3).
The experiment included four distinct conditions to explore the dynamics of
auditory attention, as shown in Fig. 3:
No manipulation
Participants were instructed to actively listen to the teacher without any
additional prompts or interruptions.
Disengagement
Participants performed an interfering task to divert their attention away
from the speaker. These tasks included solving calculation exercises,
reading a text, or counting backwards in steps of 17 starting from 994.
Distracting
External distractors were introduced, including added background noise or
a silent animal video displayed on the screen. However, the participants were still supposed to pay attention to the teacher’s voice.
Enhancing
Visual cues (a red frame and an exclamation mark) were presented to indicate
segments that would be included in the post-hoc comprehension questions,
encouraging increased attentional engagement.
Unless stated otherwise, the analyses in this work primarily focus on the ‘no manipulation’ and ‘disengagement’ conditions (white and red boxes in Fig. 3), which represent the clearest attentive (baseline) and inattentive listening state, respectively. The distracting and enhancing conditions are not removed to preserve a continuous recording, but they are ignored in the accuracy metrics.

III-B Data Acquisition and Preprocessing
EEG signals were recorded using a BioSemi Active Two system with 64 electrodes arranged according to the 10-20 system, at a sampling rate of 2048 Hz. Prior to analysis, the recordings were processed using a standard preprocessing pipeline.
To remove slow drifts and very low-frequency components, we first applied a first-order infinite impulse response (IIR) high-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 0.01 Hz. The data were then downsampled to 128 Hz to reduce computational load while preserving the relevant EEG information.
The EEG signals were further filtered to the 0.1-4 Hz frequency band proposed in [12, 13], which corresponds to typical word-rate dynamics around 2.5 Hz. This band was extracted using a fourth-order IIR bandpass filter, after which the signals were downsampled to 16 Hz for subsequent processing.
The speech envelope was adopted as the acoustic feature, motivated by previous findings showing phase-locked neural responses to speech envelope fluctuations [4, 10, 11, 12, 7, 22, 5, 13]. Envelope extraction followed the procedure described in [22], which combines a gammatone filterbank with power-law compression to approximate cochlear frequency selectivity and nonlinear loudness perception.
For consistency with the EEG processing, the extracted envelope was filtered using the same frequency band (0.1-4 Hz by default) and downsampled to 16 Hz.
III-C Evaluation Metrics
In this work, performance is evaluated based on the ability of the resulting
metrics (either the raw NET values or the HMM outputs) to discriminate between
the ‘no manipulation’ attentive and ‘disengagement’ inattentive conditions.
We assess performance along two complementary dimensions: steady-state discriminability, which quantifies how well the two conditions can be discriminated from each other over the course of the session, and transition timing, which quantifies how accurately the timing of attention-state changes is captured. The former is captured by the Area Under the Curve (AUC), while the latter is captured by the Switch Detection Time (SDT). Unless stated otherwise, AUC is used as the primary performance metric. SDT is reported only in analyses where transition timing is directly relevant.
III-C1 Area Under the Curve
The Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) provides a
ranking-based measure of separability. It can be interpreted as the probability
that a randomly selected attention metric value from the baseline (attentive) condition is larger than
a randomly selected attention metric value from the disengagement (inattentive) condition.
Formally, given samples y1y_{1} from the baseline condition and y2y_{2} from the
disengagement condition, we estimate the AUC using its rank-based (Mann-Whitney)
formulation [30, 31]:
AUC=#⁡(y1>y2)+0.5​#​(y1=y2)#⁡(y1)​#​(y2),\mathrm{AUC}=\frac{\#(y_{1}>y_{2})+0.5\,\#(y_{1}=y_{2})}{\#(y_{1})\,\#(y_{2})},
(24)
where #⁡(⋅)\#(\cdot) denotes the number of occurrences meeting the specified condition. A higher AUC value indicates stronger discrimination between the
two experimental conditions and, consequently, improved aAAD performance.

IV-A Added value of HMM
To illustrate the added value of HMM post-processing, we compare the Fisher-transformed raw NET trace with the corresponding HMM-processed trace obtained via non-causal inference, which provides an off-line estimate of the latent attentional state. Fig. 4 presents three example 75-minute sessions (NET scores computed over 1-s windows) for participants at the 75th (participant 13), 50th (participant 27), and 25th (participant 4) percentiles of AUC performance, respectively. For each participant, the upper panel displays the raw NET and the lower panel shows the HMM posterior probability of the attentive state, p⁡(S⁡(t)=A∣y⁡(0:T))p(S(t)=A\mid y(0:T)). Across subjects at different performance quantiles, the raw NET shows strong temporal variability, making it difficult to identify a clear structure over time. In contrast, the HMM output provides a smoother and more interpretable trajectory. The HMM posterior generally remains high during ‘no manipulation’ periods (white background) and decreases during ‘disengagement’ periods (red background). The former can be viewed as attentive periods and the latter as inattentive periods, although it is important to note that these should not be treated as a fully reliable ground truth. This is particularly true for the ‘no manipulation’ segments, because participants could still be inattentive during these baseline segments.

Beyond visual inspection, we quantify the benefit at the individual level using AUC. Fig. 6 reports per-participant performance for the raw NET and for the HMM outputs. Both causal and non-causal HMM inference outperform the raw NET baseline across participants, and the non-causal configuration consistently yields higher performance, as expected because it can leverage future observations when estimating the current state.
We focus this comparison on AUC rather than SDT, because the goal here is to quantify the gain in discriminability introduced by HMM post-processing. SDT is not reported for raw NET because the evaluation requires binary state predictions, whereas raw NET is a noisy evidence sequence without a natural decision threshold.
It is important to clarify that the HMM does not replace NET as an alternative decoding method. NET provides the window-wise neural evidence, while the HMM serves as a temporal post-processing stage that integrates this evidence over time by explicitly modeling state persistence. The observed performance gains should therefore be interpreted as the benefit of structured temporal integration of the same NET sequence, rather than as a comparison between independent decoding approaches.
Furthermore, the ‘causal’ configuration considered here refers only to the temporal inference stage of the HMM. The preceding steps in the pipeline, including EEG and speech preprocessing, neural decoder training, and emission distribution estimation, remain non-causal. Consequently, the reported causal performance represents an upper bound relative to a fully real-time implementation. In a strictly causal end-to-end setting, where all components operate without access to future data, performance could be lower.

IV-D Why NET is Particularly Suitable as Evidence for aAAD
The proposed HMM framework is presented using NET as the observation feature throughout this paper. Here, we justify this choice by comparing NET with two commonly used EEG-based attention markers, namely alpha power [8] and spectral entropy [10], using the same HMM framework. A key distinction lies in the type of attention captured by each of these features. NET directly reflects neural tracking of the attended speech stimulus and therefore provides a clear and consistent measure of auditory attention to a specific target speech signal. In contrast, alpha power and entropy are more general neural markers that have been linked to overall attention in a broader sense (e.g., arousal or cognitive effort), but that are not specifically tied to attention toward a particular auditory source.
Specifically, alpha power is defined as the mean band power of the EEG signal in the 8-12 Hz range [8], averaged across all electrodes. It is commonly used as a marker of attentional state [8, 9], although the direction of modulation can vary across individuals and paradigms [11]. Spectral entropy reflects the regularity of the EEG signal and is commonly computed from the power spectrum over a broad frequency range (0.5-32 Hz in [10, 11]). The power spectrum, estimated using Welch’s method, is first normalized to form a probability distribution. Spectral entropy is then computed as
[10, 11]
SE=−∑kpklog2pk,SE=-\sum_{k}p_{k}\log_{2}p_{k},
(27)
where pkp_{k} denotes the normalized power at frequency bin kk. Higher spectral entropy indicates a more uniform spectral distribution, whereas lower values reflect a stronger concentration of power in specific frequency bands. Both alpha power and spectral entropy are computed per analysis window using the same window lengths as NET and averaged across all electrodes, but notably they do not use the speech signal in their computation. As a result, their relationship with auditory attention is ambiguous, and the direction of modulation (relative to the other conditions or tasks) is not well defined, which makes it hard to assign class labels in an unsupervised setting. In the proposed fully unsupervised GMM-based emission estimation for NET, the component with the larger mean is assigned to the attentive state. This assignment is naturally justified, as higher neural tracking scores consistently indicate stronger auditory attention. However, the same assignment is not necessarily valid for alpha power and entropy, for which the direction of modulation may even vary across participants. To provide a fair comparison, we determine the correct direction for each feature using the ground-truth labels, i.e., based on the average ordering between attentive and inattentive segments across all participants. Specifically, higher alpha power and lower entropy are associated with attentive state, and this is used consistently in the HMM model. However, we note that this is based on the average across participants, and this direction is not always fully consistent across participants.
We compare the three features using non-causal HMM inference with the
same multiscale emission estimation procedure and transition probabilities
as in the preceding analysis. We consider window lengths of 1, 5, 10,
15, and 30 s. AUC and SDT are computed as described in
Section III. The figure shows SDT over transitions detected
by each feature.
Fig. 9: Comparison of HMM decoding performance using NET, alpha power,
and spectral entropy across analysis window lengths. (a) Mean AUC,
with shading indicating ±1\pm 1 SEM across 30 participants; the dashed
line marks chance level (AUC = 0.5). (b) Individual SDT.
(c) Group SDT. Each SDT curve uses transitions detected by the
corresponding feature. SDT shading indicates 95% confidence
intervals obtained by bootstrapping participants.
Fig. 9 summarizes the feature comparison.
NET achieves the highest mean AUC across all tested window lengths
(Fig. 9a), whereas alpha power and spectral
entropy show weaker discriminability. At the default 1-s setting,
the mean AUCs are 0.832, 0.628, and 0.607, respectively. NET also yields
the lowest individual and group SDT across all window lengths
(Fig. 9b and c). At 1 s, individual SDT is
25.95 s for NET, 37.52 s for alpha power, and 44.60 s for spectral
entropy; the corresponding group SDTs are 18.00 s, 45.00 s (the
optimal split falls at the left search boundary because the mean
posterior stays below 0.5), and 40.75 s. The individual miss rates
are 29.0%, 30.5%, and 28.6%, respectively, while the numbers of
missed group transitions are zero, three, and three out of seven. These results support the use of
NET as the observation feature in the proposed unsupervised
HMM framework: unlike alpha power and spectral entropy,
NET is stimulus-specific and has a well-defined direction with
respect to auditory attention to the target speech.
V Conclusion
We have presented a practical, modular pipeline for unsupervised absolute auditory attention decoding (aAAD) in single-speaker listening scenarios. The proposed pipeline extracts a windowed neural envelope tracking (NET) sequence as stimulus-specific evidence and applies an HMM for probabilistic temporal inference, enabling continuous attention tracking without relying on explicit attention labels. Across all participants, HMM post-processing consistently improves the separability between ‘no manipulation’ (attentive) and ‘disengagement’ (inattentive) periods compared to the raw NET trace, yielding a more interpretable attention trajectory. We further investigate the effect of analysis window length on AUC and SDT. Compared with MA smoothing, the HMM achieves higher discriminability across the examined smoothing scales. Although the individual SDTs of the two methods are comparable, the HMM provides lower group-level SDT over most smoothing scales after participant averaging. Finally, we show that NET outperforms alpha power and spectral entropy in terms of AUC within the proposed framework, supporting its use as the observation feature for HMM-based attention tracking.

The data supporting the findings of this study are not publicly available and are not available for external sharing.

All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. The study was conducted in accordance with the relevant ethical guidelines and regulations of the SMEC.

sections.heading: 课堂实验的操作分段和评价规则
sections.body:
实验有三十名成人被试，看七十五分钟关于神经迷思的视频讲座，只有一位教师对着幻灯片讲解。视频分成八段，第一段五分钟、其余每段十分钟，段间有短暂休息。每三十秒一个小格，共四种操作：无操作要求主动听讲，分心段要求做算术、阅读或从九九四倒数十七等干扰任务，干扰段加背景噪声或无声动物视频但仍要求听老师，增强段用红框感叹号提示后续有理解题。默认评价只用无操作基线段和分心段，前者当专注参考，后者当不专注参考，增强和干扰段保留以保持记录连续但不计入准确率。脑电用六十四导按十到二十系统以二千零四十八赫兹记录。评价有两个维度：曲线下面积是随机取一个基线分数大于随机取一个分心分数的概率，按曼惠特尼秩式计算，越大越好；切换检测时间是把连续后验插值到一秒网格、零点五阈值二值化后，在真值切换前后四十五秒内搜索最吻合的候选翻转时刻，估计时刻与真值时刻的绝对差，越小越好，找不到有效候选记为漏检，漏检不计入切换检测时间但会影响曲线下面积。个体切换检测时间是每人对检出转折取中位数再跨人平均，群体切换检测时间是先跨人平均轨迹再对检出转折取平均，置信区间都用一千次被试自助法得到。
